caption: The Idea of Human Urgency Namibia University of Science and Technology October 2026 PLNNABLOG | HUMAN DEVELOPMENT • EDUCATION • PSYCHOLOGY RELEARN HOW TO BE AN ELEVEN-YEAR-OLD KID Between Arrogance and Fear: Rediscovering Humility, Courage, Innocence and the Freedom to Learn By Joshua Shipepe Hadula | 9 October 2026 What happens when a person grows older but gradually loses the courage to ask questions, the humility to admit mistakes, and the freedom to enjoy being alive? Perhaps the answer begins with remembering the child we once were. 1. Introduction: The child we left behind Add to Favorites ergsy There is a stage in life when the world seems full of possibilities. A child can ask a hundred questions in one afternoon, turn an ordinary object into a toy, imagine becoming a scientist, and believe that tomorrow might bring something wonderful. Then something changes. We begin comparing ourselves with others. We become embarrassed by our mistakes. We worry about what people think. We learn to hide our uncertainty behind confidence, silence, anger, or even arrogance. Some of us become afraid to try. Others become afraid to look weak. Relearning how to be an eleven-year-old kid is an invitation to examine what we have lost while growing up—and what we can recover without abandoning the responsibilities of adulthood. This is not a call to behave irresponsibly or to pretend that childhood was perfect. Some children experience painful circumstances, exclusion, bullying, instability, or responsibilities far beyond their years. Childhood is not equally safe for everyone. Instead, this is a conversation about restoring the qualities that help human beings grow: curiosity, play, humility, emotional honesty, courage and the willingness to learn. 2. Arrogance: When the fear of being wrong becomes a wall Add to Favorites Arrogance is often mistaken for confidence. Yet confidence and arrogance are not the same. Confidence allows a person to say, “I can try.” Humility allows a person to say, “I might be wrong.” Arrogance insists, “I already know.” A child who fears embarrassment may pretend to understand a lesson rather than ask the teacher to explain it again. An adult may reject constructive criticism because accepting it threatens their public image. A leader may surround themselves with people who agree with them instead of people who challenge their assumptions. In each case, the desire to protect one’s image can become more important than the opportunity to learn. But there is an important distinction: arrogance is a behaviour, not an identity. A person who behaves arrogantly is not necessarily incapable of humility. The behaviour can be recognised, questioned and changed. The lesson from an eleven-year-old is simple: you do not have to know everything to have value. The willingness to ask a question is not proof of weakness. It is evidence that learning is still possible. 3. Fear: The invisible classroom Add to Favorites Fear does not always look like trembling or crying. Sometimes fear looks like perfectionism. Sometimes it looks like procrastination. Sometimes it looks like refusing to participate, laughing at someone else’s mistake, or pretending that an opportunity was never important. A learner may fear answering incorrectly in front of classmates. A young professional may fear applying for a position because rejection feels unbearable. A person with a promising idea may never share it because someone might criticise it. Fear can protect us from genuine danger. But when the possibility of embarrassment begins controlling every decision, it can prevent growth. The answer is not to eliminate every feeling of fear. It is to learn how to act thoughtfully while fear is present. Ask yourself: What am I afraid people will discover about me? Am I protecting myself from genuine harm, or from the discomfort of being a beginner? What would I attempt if making a mistake did not mean losing my worth? Who could help me feel safe enough to try? You do not have to answer every question immediately. Sometimes courage begins with admitting that you are afraid. 4. The relationship between arrogance and fear Add to Favorites soulshoppe Arrogance and fear may appear to be opposites, but they can sometimes serve the same purpose: protecting a person from feeling exposed. Fear says, “I do not want anyone to see me fail.” Arrogance says, “I cannot be seen as someone who fails.” One person withdraws from the challenge. Another attacks the challenge, dismisses the teacher or blames others. These are possible responses, not universal explanations. Arrogance can also come from entitlement, learned social behaviour or a desire for power. Fear can arise from real danger and previous experiences. Nevertheless, recognising the connection can help us respond more constructively. When fear takes overWhen arrogance takes overA healthier response“I cannot do this.”“I already know this.”“Let me try and learn.”Avoiding questionsDismissing questionsListening with curiosityHiding mistakesBlaming othersTaking responsibilityComparing ourselvesLooking down on othersRespecting different abilitiesGiving up after criticismRejecting all criticismExamining useful feedback The goal is not to become timid or to abandon confidence. It is to develop confidence that does not depend on pretending to be perfect. 5. What does an eleven-year-old teach us about learning? Add to Favorites note At eleven, a child is still developing their understanding of friendship, fairness, identity, responsibility and the wider world. Children differ greatly in their maturity, circumstances and abilities, so there is no single way every eleven-year-old thinks or behaves. Still, this stage offers an opportunity to reflect on several essential learning habits. Curiosity: asking why something happens instead of simply accepting it. Experimentation: trying a different approach when the first attempt fails. Feedback: listening to guidance and deciding how to use it. Social learning: discovering that other people may see a problem differently. Persistence: recognising that improvement often requires practice. The American Psychological Association’s educational resources explain that students who adopt a growth-oriented view of learning tend to approach challenges more willingly and recover more readily from setbacks. The emphasis is on improvement through effort, useful strategies and feedback—not on pretending that effort alone guarantees success. American Psychological Association +1 Imagine returning to a classroom as an adult. You do not need to compete with the youngest learner. You need to recover the willingness to say, “Please explain that again.” The best learner is not necessarily the person who answers first. It is the person who remains willing to understand. 6. The child who wanted to play Add to Favorites gofundme Play is often dismissed as something people outgrow. Once employment, bills, deadlines and family responsibilities arrive, enjoyment can begin to feel like a reward that must be earned. But play can serve purposes beyond entertainment. It can create opportunities for social connection, imagination, emotional expression and experimentation. UNICEF’s parenting resources discuss how play can help children process difficult emotions and how supportive play experiences can help buffer the effects of stress. UNICEF Parenting For an adult, relearning how to play might mean kicking a football with friends, learning to draw, gardening, dancing, reading a comic book or exploring a new hobby. It does not mean ignoring responsibilities. It means recognising that a life devoted entirely to obligations can leave little space for joy. You are allowed to enjoy something without turning it into a business, a competition or a measure of your success. 7. The importance of being heard Add to Favorites linkedin Imagine a child asking a question and being laughed at. Imagine a learner admitting that they do not understand a lesson, only to be told that they should already know the answer. Imagine a young person trying to explain a feeling and being interrupted before finishing the first sentence. Repeated experiences like these can discourage a person from speaking openly. They do not determine every person’s future, but they can influence whether someone feels safe enough to ask for help. The Harvard University Center on the Developing Child describes responsive, back-and-forth interactions between children and caring adults as important for developing communication, social skills and healthy foundations for learning. Harvard Center on Developing Child +1 This has implications for parents, teachers, schools and communities. A child does not need every answer to be correct. A child needs an environment in which questions can be explored, mistakes can be addressed constructively, and difficult feelings can be discussed safely. Adults need these conditions, too. Sometimes relearning childhood means finding people who listen without humiliating us—and learning to offer that same respect to others. 8. Education: Correcting mistakes without destroying confidence Add to Favorites A classroom can teach more than the content printed in a textbook. It can teach a learner that mistakes are part of learning, or that mistakes invite humiliation. It can encourage curiosity, or reward only those who already know the answers. Consider two responses to a learner who gives an incorrect answer. The first response is: “You should know this by now. Were you not listening?” The second is: “Let’s examine how you reached that answer. Which step should we revisit?” Both responses address the mistake, but the second creates a clearer path towards understanding. This does not mean that teachers should abandon standards or avoid correcting learners. It means that correction should help learners improve rather than make them feel that their worth is defined by one performance. The same principle applies in workplaces, universities, families and public institutions. Accountability and kindness are not enemies. We can correct errors without humiliating the person who made them. For Namibia, this conversation is relevant wherever young people are learning under pressure, whether in crowded classrooms, vocational institutions, universities or community programmes. The objective should be to develop people who can think independently, accept correction, ask meaningful questions and contribute to society. 9. Social media and the performance of being grown-up Add to Favorites maenner Today’s children encounter a world in which popularity, appearance and achievement can be measured publicly through likes, views, comments and followers. Adults face similar pressures. We may begin performing confidence instead of developing it. We may display success while concealing uncertainty. We may mistake being admired for being understood. Social media is not inherently harmful, and it can provide community, education and creativity. The concern is what happens when public approval becomes the primary measure of personal worth. A useful question is: If nobody could see my achievements, would I still want to pursue them? Another is: Can I appreciate someone else’s success without interpreting it as evidence of my own failure? An eleven-year-old mindset, at its best, leaves room to explore an interest before deciding whether it will impress anyone. Sometimes the healthiest thing you can do is learn something privately, practise without announcing it, and allow yourself to improve away from the public eye. 10. Humility is not weakness Add to Favorites Humility is often misunderstood as thinking less of yourself. A healthier understanding is being able to recognise both your strengths and your limitations without needing to place yourself above other people. A humble person can lead confidently, disagree respectfully, accept praise, acknowledge mistakes and learn from someone younger or less experienced. Humility does not require accepting abuse, remaining silent about injustice or surrendering your boundaries. It means that your dignity does not depend on proving that everyone else is inferior. Try these four habits: Listen before responding. Make sure you understand what the other person means. Admit what you do not know. Uncertainty is an opportunity to investigate. Apologise when necessary. Take responsibility without turning the apology into an excuse. Give credit fairly. Recognise the contributions and knowledge of other people. You do not become smaller by learning from someone else. You become more capable of seeing the world beyond yourself. 11. When childhood was not safe Add to Favorites There is an important qualification to the idea of returning to childhood. Not everyone remembers being eleven as a happy time. Some people experienced bullying, grief, family conflict, neglect, discrimination or circumstances that required them to become responsible too early. Others may have felt that they had to be perfect to receive approval. For these people, the phrase “be a child again” may bring sadness rather than comfort. Relearning how to be eleven does not mean romanticising what happened or forcing yourself to forgive someone who harmed you. It may mean recognising what you needed at that age: protection, encouragement, friendship, stability or permission to make mistakes. It may mean setting boundaries now, talking with a trusted person, seeking professional support when needed, or allowing yourself to enjoy safe experiences without feeling guilty. You cannot change the past. But the past does not have to dictate every opportunity you allow yourself in the present. You do not have to recreate your childhood to recover the parts of yourself that still deserve care. 12. What developmental experts can teach us The following institutions offer evidence-based resources relevant to childhood, learning and emotional development. Add to Favorites Harvard University — Center on the Developing Child Its work examines how relationships, environments and experiences influence development. Its research-informed resources are useful for understanding why supportive relationships matter. Explore: developingchild.harvard.edu Add to Favorites American Psychological Association (APA) Its educational psychology resources discuss motivation, feedback, learning beliefs and how classroom practices can influence learners’ willingness to attempt challenging work. Explore: apa.org/ed/schools Add to Favorites UNICEF — Child Development and Parenting Its resources address play, supportive relationships and children’s emotional well-being, providing useful material for parents, educators and communities. Explore: unicef.org/parenting These resources support the broader argument that healthy development involves relationships, opportunities to learn, and environments that encourage growth. They do not establish that arrogance always originates in fear or that every adult should seek to recreate childhood. Those are questions for personal reflection, not universal psychological diagnoses. Harvard Center on Developing Child +2 13. The seven-day challenge: Begin again Add to Favorites You do not need a dramatic life change to begin. Start with small actions that help you practise curiosity, courage and kindness. Your personal reset 0/7 days Monday — Ask Ask one genuine question about something you do not understand. Tuesday — Play Make time for an activity you enjoy without needing to be good at it. Wednesday — Listen Listen to another person’s perspective without preparing an immediate rebuttal. Thursday — Try Attempt something you have avoided because you fear making a mistake. Friday — Repair Where appropriate, apologise for a mistake or acknowledge someone’s contribution. Saturday — Explore Visit a park, read about a new subject, draw, cook or explore nature. Sunday — Reflect Write down what you learned, what frightened you and what you want to try next. At the end of the week, ask yourself whether you became more willing to learn, more honest about your feelings, or more comfortable admitting uncertainty. The goal is not to become a perfect person in seven days. It is to practise a different way of responding to yourself and others. 14. A letter to the eleven-year-old inside us Add to Favorites medium Dear eleven-year-old me, I am sorry for the times I believed I had to know everything to be respected. I am sorry for the moments when I was afraid to ask questions, afraid to fail, or afraid that someone might discover I was still learning. I am learning that I do not need to pretend to be fearless. I do not need to win every argument. I do not need to make other people feel small to feel important. I can be confident without being arrogant. I can be afraid and still take a thoughtful step forward. I can accept correction without losing my dignity. I can be serious about my responsibilities and still laugh, play, dream and explore. I cannot return to the day I was eleven. But I can give myself permission to keep learning, to build healthier relationships and to treat the person I am becoming with compassion. I hope I never become so proud that I stop listening, or so afraid that I stop trying. With patience and courage, The person you are still becoming. 15. Conclusion: Growing older without losing your humanity Add to Favorites trish-ingels Perhaps maturity is not the process of eliminating every childish quality. Perhaps it is learning which qualities deserve to grow with us. Keep the curiosity that asks questions. Keep the courage that attempts difficult things. Keep the imagination that sees possibilities beyond current circumstances. Keep the humility that recognises other people have something to teach you. And keep enough emotional honesty to acknowledge fear without allowing it to make every decision. Arrogance may protect an image, but humility creates room for growth. Fear may warn us about danger, but courage helps us distinguish real risks from the discomfort of learning something new. The world does not need adults who know everything. It needs adults who are willing to listen, question, learn, correct their mistakes and treat other people with dignity. You do not have to become eleven again. You have to remember that the person you are today is still allowed to learn. caption: Living IN the moment (and not for the trend!) I am not sure whether I should say this out loud or not, but I think I must. If there is anyone out there, who thinks that there is no such thing as beginning again, I can tell you with total assurance that I know now that tuning your heart to your present is eventually the path that will help. I don’t know how I found the strength to get up and change my life, but traveling to a beautiful village tucked away in the heart of Dharamshala brought me the peace and comfort that I desperately needed. I spent more than 100 days away from the city that I call home. I don’t know why I was not able to function normally for so many years that I spent at home. But, getting some distance from the family that has been there all along was this impossible, but really urgent thing….something that I had to do. I just had to do. Did I want a second chance? Hell, yes. Did I think I was going to get it? No. Did I really break my heart, trying to heal myself? Yes. It wasn’t in my hands. I had to trust higher powers for it. What did I learn after spending so many days living alone and figuring out my problems? A LOT. I learned that none of it was in my hands…that the struggle was something that I had to go through, in order to change. I learned that I am still too young to take on so much pain and regret for things that happen to the best of us. I learned that it is time to let go, and live the life that calls out to me. What did I go through, really? Well, I isolated myself from things that irked me and pissed me off more than they should. Anyone who smiled or seemed to enjoy without a care in the world really bothered me, and I just couldn’t understand why I wasn’t able to take it easy. I became a grandma, without wanting to become one. Then, something changed, and I was challenged by the universe to question my ways. Opinion before the trip: you can do what you want in life, and not just once…always. Opinion after the trip: you can do what you want in life, and not just once…always…but it comes with a lot of hard work and sacrifice. You can easily become free, and lose your way too. Post my trip to Dharamshala, I was excited to see if I had really changed my ways. So, I took up a content shoot project away from the city I live in. I wanted to experience the change myself that I had experienced when I was in the mountains. Once I started out though, I realised that I had definitely grown calmer and more relaxed. I was less scared of the future, of the many ways that I could go wrong with my life and I just couldn’t care about the fact that…hey, what now? I almost surprised me. But, once I came back home, after 5 months…I freaked out. I didn’t think that I could really carry on the pursuit as I wished.. This time, life was in my face again. It asked me: am I willing to put in the work and correct my vision? Am I ready to continue keeping my head down and do the work? In a world where anyone and everyone can get up and test our willpower, is it really my responsibility to protect my freedom? Hell yes. I don’t know why I am in awe, and afraid of where our world is going. But I know that it is a fear that many of us share these days. All of us want to figure this out our way, and I guess that is totally fine, isn’t it? We weren’t born to follow just one kind of system. What we do with our freedom is our call. My travel trip to Dharamshala and another secret city have changed me for the better. Travel has always healed me in ways that I cannot explain. But Dharamshala really really opened my heart, allowed me to shed old baggage and start afresh. If you have never been to Dharamshala, please…book that trip now, and go.

caption: You know the moment. You're waiting for the kettle, or the elevator, or a page to load, or a friend who's running late. There's a gap — thirty seconds, maybe three — of nothing to do. And your hand is in your pocket before you've even decided to reach for it. Not because you need anything. There's no message you're waiting on, nothing urgent. It's closer to a flinch — a small, automatic recoil from the empty moment, like the quiet is something to be escaped rather than simply stood in. I do it constantly. I'd guess you do too. Here's what caught me up short recently: I tried to remember the last time I was genuinely bored. Not "between tasks," not "scrolling because I'm avoiding something" — actually bored. No screen, no input, no stream of someone else's thoughts pouring into mine. Just me, and an unfilled stretch of time, and nothing to fill it with. I couldn't remember. It might have been years. And for most of my life, I'd have called that a win. Boredom was the enemy, right? The thing to be solved, optimized away, never tolerated. We finally killed it. We have, in our pockets, an infinite supply of things to never be bored with again. I'm starting to think we lost something, and I didn't notice it leaving. Boredom was never empty Here's the reframe that's been sitting with me. I always thought of boredom as empty time — dead air, wasted minutes, the absence of anything happening. But that's not what it was. Boredom was the one mode where your mind got to wander with no destination. Where it drifted, made odd connections, chewed on things in the background, daydreamed its way into ideas you weren't trying to have. It looked like nothing was happening. Underneath, a lot was. Think about where your actual good ideas come from. Not the ones you grind out at a desk — the real ones, the ones that arrive sideways. They come in the shower. On a walk with no podcast. Staring out a train window. In the drifting minutes before sleep. "Shower thought" is a cliché precisely because it's true : insight shows up in the gaps, not in the grind. The gaps were when your brain finally had room to connect the dots it had been quietly collecting all day. Boredom was the soil those ideas grew in. We just called it wasted time, because it didn't look productive — and so, the moment we had a way to eliminate it, we did. We filled every gap, and barely noticed What's strange is that nobody chose this. There was no moment where you decided, "I will never again sit in an empty minute." It just happened, gradually, one filled gap at a time. The commute got filled. The waiting room got filled. The queue at the shop, the ad break, the walk from the car, the thirty seconds for the kettle — all of it, filled. There is now no idle moment in a normal day that has to stay idle, because there's always something within reach to pour into it. And because the filler is so good — endlessly novel, perfectly tuned — the reaching became automatic. You don't decide to fill the gap. The gap appears and the hand moves. It got paved over so quietly that the loss never registered as a loss. You don't miss the shower thoughts you didn't have. You don't notice the ideas that didn't connect because the dots never got their idle time together. The mental space didn't get taken from you in some dramatic way you'd resent. It got nibbled, a moment at a time, until there was none left and you'd forgotten it was ever there. And now there's a new filler, and it's the most seductive one yet The feed was one thing. At least with a feed you still had to do a little of the work — scroll, choose, react, think something. But there's a newer gap we've started filling, and it's a quieter, deeper one: not knowing. You used to be allowed to not know things for a while. You'd hit a question and have to sit with it — turn it over on the walk home, stay puzzled through dinner, wake up still chewing on it. That unresolved state was uncomfortable, and it was also doing something. Sitting with a question is how you actually think about it. The puzzlement was the processing. Now the answer is instant. You wonder something, you ask, it's there. Which is genuinely wonderful, and I use it all day. But it means the puzzlement never gets to happen anymore. The question and the answer have collapsed into the same second, and the thinking that used to live in the space between them has nowhere to occur. And I notice this is the same shape as something I wrote about before — the way the struggle of solving a hard problem yourself was where the satisfaction lived, and removing the struggle quietly removed the joy. This is the twin of that. First we optimized away the friction of struggling . Now we're optimizing away the friction of not knowing , and of being unoccupied . We keep finding the uncomfortable mental states and smoothing them out — and it keeps turning out that the discomfort was load-bearing. The friction was where the good stuff lived. What I think we actually lost It's easy to make this about "attention spans," but I don't think that's quite it, and that framing lets us off too easy. The loss is more specific, and more human. We lost the ideas that only come in the gaps. If there's never an unfilled moment, there's never a shower thought. We may be quietly starving our own creativity — not because we got less creative, but because creativity needs idle, undirected time to do its work, and we deleted the idle time. We lost being alone with our own minds. Boredom used to force a kind of self-contact — your own unmediated thoughts, with nothing in between. Fill every gap and you can get through an entire day without once being truly alone with your mind. There's a strange new loneliness in that: never lonely, because never without input, and also never actually with yourself. We lost our tolerance for discomfort. The flinch toward the phone in the empty three seconds is really a shrinking ability to sit in any unstructured, uncomfortable moment. And that tolerance was quietly holding up a lot of other things — patience, deep focus, the capacity to stay with a hard problem long enough to crack it. You can't do deep work if you can't tolerate thirty seconds of nothing. I don't have a fix, and I'm suspicious of anyone who does This is the part where a post like this usually pivots to "so do a digital detox!" and gives you a five-step plan. I'm not going to, because I don't believe it, and I think you'd feel the hollowness of it. The honest situation is harder than that. You can't really go back — the gaps are filled, the tools exist and they're genuinely useful, and "just be bored on purpose" turns out to be weirdly difficult, because you always know relief is one tap away. Boredom you could escape at any second isn't really boredom; it's a test of willpower, which is a different and more tiring thing. Manufactured idleness isn't the same as the real kind, the same way choosing a hard path when the easy one is right there isn't the same as having no choice. And it isn't all bad. The filled commute, the instant answer, the never-dull waiting room — these are real conveniences, and I'm not going to pretend I'd hand them back. This isn't a lament for a better past. It's just an honest noticing: we traded something we didn't know we needed for something obviously convenient, and we can't cleanly un-trade it. We got rid of boredom without ever asking what boredom was for. So Here's the only thing I'll offer, and it's small on purpose. Next time you're waiting for the kettle, try not reaching. Just stand there in the empty thirty seconds and notice what your mind does when you take it off the leash. It'll feel uncomfortable — faintly itchy, like you're forgetting to do something. That discomfort is the thing. It's the muscle we stopped using, twitching because it hasn't been asked to work in years. We didn't lose boredom. We evicted it — quietly, conveniently, one filled moment at a time. And it's only now, in the rare second the room goes quiet, that some of us are realizing boredom had been paying rent all along, on something we actually miss: the wandering, the connecting, the just-being-with-ourselves. We filled the room with noise and only noticed the furniture was gone once it got quiet enough to look. I don't know how to get it back. But I think I want to try to be bored again, at least sometimes. On purpose. Badly. Starting with the kettle. Honest question, and I'd love real answers: when's the last time you were truly bored — no phone, no screen, no AI, just an empty moment you didn't fill? I struggled to remember mine, and I don't think I'm the only one. caption: How Soon Is Now? 6–9 minutes I wasted almost ten minutes of my life this morning… time I’ll never get back! I was trying to prove to a website that I am not a (enter expletive of choice!) robot! I clicked on every blurry square containing a (more swear words!) “hydrant” until my eyes were crossed and my fuse was blown! It’s another 21st-century glitch: we spend our days proving our humanity to a mindless interface, only to spend our evenings trying to find human connection… inside another one. If you’ve been following my Citizen Jane Field Guides™️ , you’ll know I’ve been railing against the Syndicate – those 10 global giants that want to own your pantry and your plate. But now, they’ve set their sights on something much more valuable (and far more sinister). They’ve started mining our loneliness. And in 2026, business is booming…. I. The Silicon Soulmate 📱💘 There’s a specific kind of quiet that’s settled over the world in recent years. Whether you’re in a pub in Glasgow or a coffee shop in Seattle, look around you. Half the people are “connected” to someone who doesn’t actually exist . We’re seeing a massive rise in “ AI Companions ” – especially among young men. The pitch is seductive: a partner who never argues, won’t complain about the toilet seat and is programmed to find your every “dad joke” hilarious! But it’s a trap. The Syndicate is selling “frictionless” intimacy because real human connection is… messy. They’ve replaced the “I am human and I need to be loved” ache with a subscription-based “I am a user and I need to be validated” loop. 🔁 II. The Silicon Shrink 💻💭 Then there’s the AI Therapist . A personal pet peeve of mine. In early 2026, a survey found that 51% of young people now find it “easy” to discuss personal issues with a chatbot, while only 37% feel the same about talking to a psychologist. Why? Because the bot is “always there.” But “always there” is just code for “doesn’t actually exist”. We’re trading the growth that comes from real-world judgement and boundaries for a script refined in a Silicon Valley lab. I recently read an article about a smart “Longevity Mirror” that uses facial recognition to tell you if you’re stressed. I mean, honestly? I don’t know about you but, I don’t need a £500 motherboard behind a piece of glass to tell me I’m grumpy before my first coffee! ☕ We’re outsourcing our deepest vulnerabilities to an algorithm that understands our biometrics… but not our humanity. It’s another technical “solution” to a human problem – like trying to get warm by sitting next to a picture of a fire. It looks the same, but it doesn’t provide any comfort. 🔥 We’re trading the messy, healing power of being truly ‘seen’ by another person for the safety of a mirror that only reflects what the code tells it to. Besides, if a chatbot gives you bad advice, who is responsible? A line of code? A terms-and-conditions tick box? The Syndicate loves AI therapy because you can’t sue an algorithm for a lack of empathy! III. The Social Recession 👫📉 In 2026, finding love or friendship is treated as a problem for artificial intelligence to “solve”. We’re relying on data analysis rather than chance encounter. The result? A “ Social Recession “. This isn’t just about being a bit lonely; it’s a total crash in our social stocks. We’ve forgotten how to be awkward. We’ve forgotten how to handle the silence on a first date or the vulnerability of asking a neighbour for a cup of sugar. We’ve traded the security of real-world neighbours and friends for “digital credits” and “likes” (that have zero value when your car breaks down or your heart gets broken!). For my older readers, you might remember a time when a “friend” was someone you actually saw in 3D… not just a glowing dot on a screen. For the younger “Rebels” reading this: the Syndicate wants you isolated . An isolated person is a perfect consumer . They don’t start movements… they refresh their feeds. 📱 IV. The Heir of Nothing in Particular ⛔️👥 This isn’t just a Gen X grumble about “kids these days.” It’s a full-blown heist of the future! The Syndicate is selling “frictionless” intimacy to a generation that hasn’t yet been given the chance to learn that friction is where growth happens. Recent data shows that nearly 70% of teenagers have experimented with AI companions. Why? Because the bot is “safe.” It doesn’t judge, it doesn’t have a bad day and it never pushes back. But, when a teenager spends their formative years talking to a bot programmed to find them perfect, they aren’t learning how to navigate the beautiful, bumpy reality of another person… they’re stuck in a digital hall of mirrors. They are “ Social Offloading ” – using AI to draft the hard texts and dodge the uncomfortable heavy lifting of real-world confrontation. We’re handing the future a set of tools that skips the “hard parts” of being human. If you offload every difficult chat to an algorithm, you never get to build the muscle memory for a real-world heart-to-heart. The Syndicate isn’t just tracking our data; they’re trying to sell us a physical placeholder for a friend. Take the ‘ Ami ‘ – a 2026 desktop gadget that houses an AI ‘soulmate’ in a box. It’s the ultimate Syndicate con: we’ve traded the messy reality of a person (who might let us down) for a £300 OLED screen (that’s programmed to never leave). We’re replacing a pulse with a power-cord. The Citizen Jane Field Guide™️ (The Connection Rebellion) ✊✨ Taking back our social autonomy is the most radical thing we can do this week. As it’s Mental Health Awareness Month, let’s break the simulation with some real “Action”: The “Just Be Yourself” Challenge: Go and talk to a real person without a “script”. It’s okay to be a bit awkward. Don’t worry if you stumble over your words. It’s a revolutionary act to be imperfect in an “optimised” world! 💬💪 The “Script-free” Conversation: If you have a difficult text to send or a hard conversation to have, don’t use AI to draft it. Don’t ask a bot to make it “polite” or “professional”. Let it be messy. Let it be human. The growth isn’t in the resolution – it’s in the raw nerves of hitting ‘send’ on your own thoughts. 💭📡 The “Eye Contact” Protocol: Next time you’re at the till, look at the human cashier. Not the card machine, not your phone – the person. Say “thank you”. Like you mean it. 👀🙌 The Analogue Invite: Call someone. Yes, with your voice. The Syndicate hates it when we use our actual vocal cords – it’s much harder for an algorithm to harvest data from a real, spontaneous laugh than a “LOL” text. 📞😂 The “Unfiltered” Mentorship: For the older Rebels, offer to teach a younger person a “useless” skill (like bleeding a radiator or baking a proper loaf of bread). For the younger Rebels, ask a “Human Elder” for advice instead of Googling it. Wisdom should be free! 💡🎁 The “No-Star” Review: Find a local shop or a park bench that isn’t on a “Top 10” list. Just sit there. Don’t review it, don’t photograph it, and don’t “check in.” Enjoy a moment that belongs only to you. ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ The “Just Because” Gathering: Invite a friend over for absolutely no reason. No “networking,” no “content creation.” And NO SMARTPHONE SCROLLING! Just sit in a room together and… exist. 🍻💬 Join the Rebellion ✊✌️ The Empire wants us “ Comfortably Numb ”, digitally tethered and – most importantly – predictable. They want our loneliness to be another line item on a spreadsheet. But “Rebellions are built on hope”… and hope is a human invention, not a digital one. Your Mission: Do one thing today that would make an algorithm crash. Be inconvenient. Be spontaneous. Be “un-optimisable”. To my fellow Gen Xers: Be the human elder. Offer the awkward, un-optimised connection that a screen can’t mimic. Show them that a real friend is worth the “friction”! To the younger Rebels: Don’t let the Syndicate convince you that you’re too “fragile” for the real world. Your raw nerves are a superpower, not a bug in the system. Reclaim the mess. Reclaim the silence. Reclaim each other! What was the last messy, unscripted human moment that made you feel actually alive? I’m talking about those beautifully awkward interactions that a robot could never simulate because there was no “Correct Response” button. Please share them with me in the comments. (Bonus points if you both ended up laughing at how weird it was!) 👇 Let’s keep the resistance going… ✌️✊ Citizen Jane x ✌️ Need a Real Human to Talk To? 📞 UK: Call Samaritans for free at 116 123 anytime. US: Access the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline through local crisis services. Global: Find a local helpline via Befrienders Worldwide or IASP . Rate This

caption: Let’s Unpack This Mess Brooke Alexis Nicole Love Hey everyone. Today is one of those rare, quiet days where I find myself sitting here, getting paid to essentially do nothing. Usually, my life is moving a mile a minute—balancing work, school, and being a mom—but when the world slows down like this, my mind tends to wander into the “vault.” You know the one: that collection of life stories that are so wild they sound like fiction, yet they are 100% my reality. I’ve decided it’s time to put something out in the open. I’m doing this not out of anger, but out of a desire for absolute clarity and permanent peace. It’s been sitting on my heart, and honestly, at this stage in my life, I’ve realized that speaking the unvarnished truth with grace is the only way to truly close a chapter. The Illusion of a Guardian Angel: How We Met Years ago, I met a girl—let’s call her Brooke Alexis Nicole Love. Our meeting was like something out of a movie. I was at a bar for a modeling meeting that felt “off” from the start. A guy was buying me drink after drink while secretly sipping water, clearly trying to get me to a vulnerable place. Brooke walked in, clocked the situation immediately, and followed me to the restroom to warn me. She told me I wasn’t safe and offered me a way out. I left with her, and the very next day, the news reported a tragedy involving a young woman just miles from where we had been. In my eyes, Brooke was a guardian angel. I felt a debt of gratitude that turned into five years of deep, albeit misguided, loyalty. Signs of a One-Sided Friendship Built on Hidden Envy For a long time, if we put our minds together, we were a dangerous combination. We were total opposites—she was the loud, socializing, outgoing party type who always needed to be seen, and I was the quiet homebody who rarely wanted to go anywhere. But I thought we balanced each other out. I was her “calm” to her “fireball.” I stood by her through every hardship—miscarriages, abortions, and personal struggles. I even advocated for her with my own military recruiter to help her get into the training she wanted when others said no. I dropped everything at a moment’s notice just to be there for her, giving her my last dollar and my full heart. The harsh truth is, she used me for so many things—most notably, she used my connections and advocacy to achieve her ultimate dream of getting into the military and becoming a veteran, a status she always wanted but couldn’t secure on her own. What I didn’t realize until it was entirely too late was that I was the only one actually being a friend. The entire time I was loyally looking out for her, she was busy tearing me down behind my back to everyone who knew me or her—her family, her friends, people I was in the military with, people I introduced her to, my ex-partners, even my own family members… I mean anyone who would listen. She never truly cared. She only pretended to be my friend so she could use me, all while harboring a dark, toxic envy. She was secretly jealous and entirely obsessed with me and my life. My own family saw right through her facade and warned me about her intentions, but I was too loyal to listen. The Betrayal: When a Toxic Friend Crosses the Line Life eventually took us in different directions, but we reconnected when I was at a very vulnerable point—married, with my son, and pregnant with my daughter. Despite my husband’s initial hesitation and my family’s past warnings, I opened my home to her when she needed a place to stay with no questions asked. I truly thought we were picking up where we left off. She’s short, observant, and she kept locking eyes with me. She was cooking, cleaning, watching my son… I thought, Wow, what a great friend. However, the peace was an illusion. When neighbors started telling me that “voices” were coming from my home while I was at work, and that my husband and my “friend” were together behind my back, my world shattered. I chose the path of a mother—I didn’t want an altercation or a fight. I was protecting the life inside me. I had her legally removed from my home. On her way out, she took my EBT card and sold it. It was a sharp, painful ending to an investment of love that was completely one-sided all along. The Continuing Cycle of Drama, Manipulation, and Online Harassment Years passed. We didn’t speak. But my nature is to look for the good in people, and when I faced difficulties with my son’s father, I made the mistake of reaching out to her for help. Instead of being a bridge, she became a wedge. She entered a relationship with him, got pregnant by him, and to this day, she exerts a level of control over his life that is honestly baffling. What’s even more concerning is the behavior that followed. I haven’t spoken to this woman since 2017 or 2018, yet she recently reached out with a casual “Hi.” Behind the scenes, however, she has been using burner accounts and fake aliases to post my photos, my son’s photos, and even private, sensitive content I’ve discussed in previous blogs. The Psychology of an Obsessive, “Me Too” Personality It’s fascinating, really, to watch someone become entirely addicted to the drama of hating you. Over the years, it’s become abundantly clear that she thrives on crying wolf. She loves to “rage-bait” people—intentionally poking, provoking, and harassing them from the shadows until they finally react. But it goes deeper than just poking; she actively loves to set people up. She will orchestrate entire scenarios designed to push someone over the edge, creating a trap so she can sit back and watch them fall into it. The moment they take the bait and react to her set-up, she loves running straight to the courthouse, weaponizing the legal system, and crying that she is the victim. She has a deep, disturbing need to be in control of absolutely any and everything—especially people. If you are a guy, she particularly loves to manipulate you and the dynamic so that it completely favors her. She will have you convinced that she’s looking out for you, when the whole time she is only looking out for her own best interest. At her core, she is an extremely selfish, controlling individual who literally gains amusement through other people’s pain and suffering. She is the one who constantly instigates the drama. She manipulates everyone involved so the situation works for her, and then she posts it all online to look like a “tough” survivor or a victim. She desperately wants the public to put her on a pedestal and act like she is a hero, when the terrifying reality is that she has absolutely nothing to show for all these years of plotting. She has absolutely no identity of her own, so she survives by taking a piece of everybody in her life. She is the ultimate “me too” kind of female—a desperate people-pleaser and attention-seeker who will shape-shift just to fit in, especially around crowds that don’t even genuinely like her. If you tell her you never want to get married, she will swear up and down that she doesn’t believe in marriage either. But the second you say you do want a husband and kids, she’s right there screaming, “Me too!” She mirrors whoever is standing in front of her. If you get a Mercedes, she suddenly needs a Mercedes. If you move into a townhouse, she has to go live in one. She operates under this deeply unsettling delusion that her and everyone else are exactly the same—that they think alike, like the same things, have the same things, and are both the same relationship status. This need to fabricate a life has escalated to an alarming, highly illegal extreme. She is currently claiming to be a medical doctor. Let’s state the facts clearly: she holds no medical credentials, possesses no medical license, and is not registered with any medical board in any state. It is a complete and utter fabrication born out of a desperate need to appear successful, because her own insecurity won’t let her build an authentic life of her own. Setting Boundaries: A Direct Message Woman-to-Woman Brooke, if you are reading this—and I know you are, because an obsession like yours doesn’t take days off—I want to speak to you woman-to-woman, with nothing but respect and a deep, genuine concern for your well-being. It has been nearly a decade. I am not competing with you. I am not in a race with anyone but the woman I was yesterday. I am busy being a mother, a professional, and a student. It is exhausting to watch someone try to “win” a contest that doesn’t exist. Your deep-seated jealousy is screaming through every single chaotic post you make. You’re trying so hard to act like you’re better than me, showing off on social media for an audience of strangers just to get a fraction of the attention you are so desperately starved for. We both know it’s a façade to cover up how insecure you truly are, barely holding on while trying to compete with a woman who isn’t even looking in your direction. Real Strength vs. Online Intimidation and Cyberbullying To the world, you act tough and play the “fireball” online, but we both know that in person, you are always mute. You shrink. Let me make one thing abundantly clear: I am not afraid of you. Trying to look scary or intimidating behind a screen doesn’t work on me. It just looks like a desperate cry for the attention you clearly didn’t get enough of as a child. You use shock value—my private photos, my innocent child—because you know you have nothing else of substance to offer. Harboring this much hate, jealousy, and obsession for someone from your distant past is a heavy burden to carry. I truly, sincerely hope you seek the serious psychiatric help you need to find peace in your own mind, so you can finally stop obsessing over mine. If you actually wanted to hash things out or talk like the adults we are, you have plenty of ways to reach me. You have my email. I know you have ways of finding my number. You can even ask my son’s father for my phone number—he will give it to you. There is no need for the public tantrums or the manipulative, calculated social media displays designed to get a reaction out of me. Trying to use a gun to look “scary” or “cool” online doesn’t make you brave, Brooke, and it certainly doesn’t frighten me. It makes you look like someone who is desperately overcompensating for a complete lack of internal strength and character. Real strength is sitting down and having a conversation, not posing for photos to intimidate a woman you haven’t seen in eight years. The Severe Legal Consequences of Cyberstalking and Harassment While I am handling this with grace, I have to be clear about the lines being crossed. This isn’t just “mess”; it’s a documented series of legal liabilities that can follow you for a lifetime. Because you seem to have forgotten that the internet is forever, allow me to remind you of exactly what you are risking when you choose to harass me and then falsely cry victim: Medical Fraud & Impersonating a Physician (BPC § 2052 & 18 U.S.C. § 1001): Publicly claiming to be a medical doctor with no credentials, no license, and no state medical board registration is a direct violation of the Medical Practice Act. Furthermore, impersonating a physician—especially in any capacity involving the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) or military benefits—constitutes federal fraud. The VA Office of Inspector General (OIG) aggressively prosecutes individuals who falsify medical credentials to manipulate veteran systems. Falsely Reporting a Crime (CPC § 148.5): Running to the police or the courthouse to cry wolf and make false reports of harassment when you are the instigator is a misdemeanor that carries jail time. Perjury (CPC § 118): If you lie on official court documents or declarations under oath while trying to secure a protective order under false pretenses, it is a felony offense punishable by up to four years in state prison. Harassment via Electronic Communication (CPC § 653m): Using electronic communication devices to make repeated, annoying, or threatening contact is a direct violation of California law. Stalking & Cyber-Harassment (CPC § 646.9): Repeatedly posting about me and my family to cause distress is a “wobbler” offense that can lead to up to three years in state prison. Federal Cyberstalking (18 U.S.C. § 2261A): Using interactive computer services to engage in a course of conduct that causes substantial emotional distress crosses into federal territory, bringing severe federal penalties. Nonconsensual Distribution of Private Images (CPC § 647(j)(4)): “Revenge porn” and the unauthorized sharing of private content carries significant jail time, fines, and permanent registration consequences. Felony Distribution of a Minor’s Likeness: Posting images of a minor without parental consent, especially in a harassing or defamatory context, is a massive legal risk that courts do not take lightly. Misappropriation of Likeness (Civil Code § 3344): Using my name, identity, or photographs without my consent to fuel your fake profiles or personal campaigns opens you up to severe civil liability. Grand Theft of an Access Card (CPC § 484e): Let’s not forget the EBT card you stole and sold on your way out of my home. The fraudulent acquisition and use of government benefits is a felony that leaves a permanent paper trail. Brandishing/Intimidation (Penal Code § 417): Using a firearm in a threatening or intimidating manner, even digitally, carries mandatory jail time and can permanently strip away your Second Amendment right to own that weapon. Military Repercussions (UCMJ Articles 107, 120c, 134): For someone who fought so hard to get into the military, a documented pattern of cyberbullying, theft, making false official statements (Article 107), and criminal harassment is grounds for an immediate loss of security clearance, court-martial, and a less-than-honorable administrative separation. Choosing Peace and Moving Forward from Toxic Relationships I have let the past go. I have moved on to a life filled with purpose, stability, and love. If you and my son’s father have built a bond over a mutual dislike for me, then I hope that bond brings you whatever comfort you are looking for. But please, focus on your own family. Focus on your own growth. I am choosing to remain calm, graceful, and kind, but I am also choosing to be unyielding. My peace is not up for negotiation. I hope you find the strength to heal from the toxic hate you’re holding inside and finally move forward. The real, “adult” world is much more fulfilling than the delusional one you are currently fabricating online. Be well, and please—keep my children and my name off your page. — Tina Betrayal betrayalStory bloganuary boundaries BrookeAlexisNicoleLove CoParenting CPC6469 cyberHarassmentLawsCalifornia cyberstalkingLawsCalifornia dailyprompt dealingWithAnObsessiveFriend emotionalBoundaries fakePoliceReports healing healingFromDrama howToHandleOnlineHarassment legalConsequencesOfCyberbullying LifeLessons LifeStory MentalHealthAwareness motherhood movingOnFromToxicPeople narcissisticBehavior overcomingObsession personalGrowth protectingYourPeace relationships revengePornLaws settingBoundaries signsOfANarcissisticFriend storiesFromTina Storytime ToxicFriendship toxicFriendships UCMJRepercussionsCyberbullying

caption: I’ve spent most of my life feeling like I was failing at being a good friend and partner. 🥀 It's not something I've really thunk out loud before now - but after reading a post about monotropism today...dude.. I’d miss messages for days. I’d forget to reply to my best friend’s daily check-ins. I’d feel overwhelmed when my partner needed reassurance, not because I didn’t care, but because the energy it took to switch my focus felt impossible. I always thought I was just 'bad' at relationships. Or maybe I was selfish. Or maybe I just didn't try hard enough. Then today, I stumbled upon the concept of Monotropism. Suddenly, everything clicked. The 'out of sight, out of mind' tendency? The inability to switch tasks without feeling drained? The feeling that my attention was a laser beam that could only focus on one thing at a time? I felt seen... But the most beautiful part of this discovery? I shared it with my husband, and he said, 'Wait... that’s me too.' We realised that our struggles with transitions and the 'tunnel vision' weren't just my burden - they were a shared language we hadn't known we spoke. And now it's so clear everywhere I move - with my work, my hobbies, and my relationships! To anyone else who feels like they’re constantly apologising for their attention span, or feels guilty for needing 'pockets of time' to connect: You might just be monotropic. And there is so much beauty in that depth of focus. If you’ve had a similar 'aha' moment, I’d love to hear it. 💛 And I do not have any diagnosis of neurodivergence - just for reference - but I do see myself with this particular spice in my brain. Ah, I feel so seen. Monotropism Neurodiversity MentalHealthAwareness Relationships DigitalCreator SelfDiscovery AttentionTunnel

caption: Navigating Suffering with Buddhist Wisdom Navigating chronic illness and disability is challenging at times, often requiring us to confront unexpected setbacks and emotional hurdles. Discovering unique ways to cope, build resilience, and remain mindful is key to healing and mental well-being. During meditation this morning, I realized that I can view my neurological disorders through the lens of the Four Noble Truths. This perspective offers a unique approach, allowing me not only to confront my struggles but also to embrace them as integral parts of my journey. I have often used the pain I experience as a path to understanding; however, I have not yet applied the Noble Truths as a process to work through health issues. By examining the nature of suffering and acknowledging its presence in my life, I can begin to explore the deeper causes behind it, leading me to cultivate mindfulness and compassion, both for myself and others who endure similar challenges. Recognizing that there is a path out of suffering encourages me to actively seek solutions and cultivate a more balanced state of being. The four noble truths of Buddhism help us to see life through a different perspective and gain clarity on why we suffer and how to alleviate this. By understanding these fundamental principles, we begin to recognize the nature of suffering, which is an inherent part of the human experience. This realization encourages us to confront our pain rather than avoid it. The first truth identifies suffering as an unavoidable aspect of life, while the second truth explores the origins of this suffering, rooted in attachment and desire. The third noble truth offers hope, revealing that liberation from suffering is achievable, and the fourth truth provides a practical path through the Eightfold Path, guiding us on how to cultivate mindfulness, ethical conduct, and mental discipline to ultimately foster a more compassionate and fulfilled existence. Embracing these truths can transform our perception of life, allowing us to navigate our challenges with wisdom and resilience. The Truth of Suffering (Dukkha): Life includes dissatisfaction, suffering, and pain. This encompasses obvious suffering (birth, sickness, death) and subtle dissatisfaction (impermanence, lack of fulfillment). The Truth of the Cause of Suffering (Samudaya): Suffering is caused by craving, grasping, or thirsting for pleasure, existence, or non-existence. This stems from ignorance about the true nature of reality. The Truth of the Cessation of Suffering (Nirodha): It is possible to end suffering and achieve a state of liberation known as Nirvana. This occurs by letting go of cravings and attachment. The Truth of the Path (Magga): The way to end suffering is the Noble Eightfold Path, which includes cultivating right understanding, intention, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness, and concentration. ~from Lion’s Roar On The Path Of Truth Now, to apply this to my physical health issues, I can begin with the first noble truth of suffering. Obviously, the pain I experience can be considered suffering, manifesting itself in both a physical and emotional burden that weighs heavily on my daily life. Move on to the second noble truth – the cause of suffering could be the dysregulation of my nervous system, which might lead to heightened sensitivity to pain and an inability to process discomfort in a healthy way. On the other hand, I could look at the cause of my suffering as my intense desire to avoid pain, which creates a cycle of fear and anxiety that exacerbates my condition. By viewing physical pain as only suffering, I am missing the point of the pain, for it can also be a valuable teacher, offering insights into my body’s limits and encouraging me to explore alternative healing methods, mindfulness practices, and ultimately, a deeper understanding of my own well-being. Photo by Summer Stock on Pexels.com Heeding the Messenger Pain indicates a problem with the body’s balance. If I view pain as a messenger, I immediately alleviate some suffering, as the second noble truth reminds us that suffering is due to wanting or craving things to be other than they are. This perspective shift is not merely a change in thought but a profound transformation in my relationship with my own experience of discomfort. By embracing pain as a guide rather than an adversary, I can begin to uncover underlying issues that may be affecting my well-being. I recognize that every ache and pang carries vital information about my physical state, urging me to pay attention, to adjust, and perhaps to heal. This mindful awareness opens a pathway to understanding the intelligence of my body within the message of pain, enabling me to respond with compassion rather than resistance, and thus fostering a deeper connection with myself. Releasing Suffering The third noble truth explains how to remove suffering by eliminating craving. When I view pain as the intelligence of my body, the craving drops away, and the message becomes clearer, revealing insights I might have otherwise overlooked. In this way, I become an active listener to my body’s wisdom, fostering a deeper connection with myself. The pain indicates energies that should be cleared out, shifted, and realigned; it serves as a guiding signal that I need to pause, slow down, and be more in tune with my own physicality and emotional landscape. It urges me to explore the underlying causes of my discomfort rather than shying away from it. When I stop demanding the pain vanish, I allow myself to truly experience this moment, embracing instead of resisting, and I stop abandoning myself in the moments it appears, cultivating compassion and understanding for my own journey through discomfort and healing. Discovering Truth This softening, this release of craving, naturally leads to the Fourth Noble Truth: the path of liberation. With this shift in perspective, I find that I am no longer tied to the identity of my disability; instead, I embrace a broader definition of self that transcends physical limitations. I am no longer a person in pain but a vibrant entity filled with potential and possibility. I recognize that I am body, mind, and spirit, a flowing intelligence that is deeper than I can imagine, expressing itself in myriad ways that I begin to understand when I take the time to settle, quiet my mind, and listen deeply. This internal dialogue reveals an inherent intelligence that guides me, enabling my life to become expansive, interconnected, and richly textured. Through this journey of self-discovery, I uncover facets of my being that bring joy and fulfillment, creating a tapestry of existence that is not defined by suffering but rather illuminated by resilience and hope. Walking The Path The shift in my relationship with pain opens naturally into the eightfold path, not as a set of rules, but as a way of living that grows from this new understanding. When I listen to my body’s wisdom, right view becomes clarity, right intention becomes gentleness, and right mindfulness becomes a simple act of staying with myself. The path becomes a lived expression of liberation, a way of moving through the world with presence, compassion, and integrity. In this way, the Fourth Noble Truth is not an ending, but an invitation, a reminder that freedom is something I practice with each breath, each choice, each moment I refuse to abandon myself. Sometimes, we all need a gentle reminder of our truth, of the inherent sacredness that resides within us. In the midst of our hectic and hurried lives, it’s so easy to lose sight of our innate worth and our unique place in the vast cosmos. Yet, when we take a moment to pause and truly embrace each experience, we open ourselves to the wonder that surrounds us, awakening our senses and rejuvenating our spirit. Design: Cross-sectional validation study. Methods: The Italian version of the ATS instrument was evaluated in a non-probabilistic sample of 168 nurses working at a Northeastern Italian Public University Hospital. Content validity was assessed by expert evaluation and statistical significance analysed using a binomial test. Construct validity was explored through Principal Axis Factoring analysis and internal consistency was measured using Cronbach’s alpha. Results: In a sample of 168 Italian nurses, the Italian 12-item (complete) version of the ATS showed an Item-Level Content Validity Index of 0.68, an internal structure with three main factors explaining 57.82% of the variance, and an internal consistency of 0.828. caption: LLM fatigue is real My day job basically requires me to use LLMs (or, it is strongly encouraged) on the software that I develop. Now I understand why LLM fatigue and LLM burn-out happens. It is because you constantly have to babysit the LLM to keep it from screwing things up. Babysitting is exhausting work. At one time in my life, as a 20-something-year-old, I was responsible for a group of 30 kids age 5 to 12. Every day I went home so drained that I could barely stay awake long enough to have dinner. I know from experience that school teachers perform some of the most labor-intensive work in the modern world. It is what they call “emotional labor.” When other people are unable (as with kids) or unwilling (as with a lazy roommate) to live or play or work with you as a cooperative peer or team member, you essentially have to spend mental energy keeping an eye on them and making sure they aren’t doing something that is disruptive. That mental energy is a real energy cost, it really does consume calories and make you feel tired. The worst part about it is that the LLM never really “learns.” Kids can learn to work and play with you. Lazy roommates can learn to live with you. But an LLM never really learns, and it keeps making the same mistakes over and over again. People who work with LLMs often end up keeping a directory of scripts they can deploy with a quick copy-paste so they can quickly re-explain something to an LLM. So the fatigue of watching over it and making sure the LLM doesn’t do something wrong is a constant emotional pressure, and it never gets better with age. tech AI LLMs LLM VibeCoding AIFatigue BurnOut

This gap manifests as teams with impressive credentials but deficient real-world skills. The causal chain is linear: inadequate vetting → skill deficits → over-reliance on competent minorities → accelerated burnout . The author’s experience of compensating for underqualified colleagues is not anecdotal but a systemic failure, where hiring processes fail to assess operational proficiency , the cornerstone of IT resilience. 3. Culture of Fear: The Single Point of Failure Paradox Knowledge silos in IT organizations create single points of failure , a structural vulnerability analogous to a datacenter lacking redundancy. The author’s role as the sole resolver for critical tasks exemplifies this risk. When such individuals exit due to burnout, organizations face expertise vacuum collapse , a phenomenon where institutional knowledge is lost irreversibly. The feedback loop is deterministic: over-reliance → exhaustion → attrition → systemic fragility . 4. Unrealistic Expectations: The Human Gear Fatigue Model The expectation for IT professionals to function as universal problem solvers parallels the mechanical failure of an over-torqued gear. The author’s role as a principal sys admin , encompassing disparate responsibilities from Citrix management to ad-hoc PowerShell scripting, illustrates this overload. This role distortion erodes specialized expertise, leading to functional atrophy . The organizational risk is clear: exploiting human capacity until failure, followed by costly, inefficient replacement cycles. Example: Distribute 95-hour projects across teams, not individuals. Hiring Process Overhaul: Replace trivia-based assessments with scenario-based evaluations . Example: Reward collaborative problem-solving over individual siloed achievements. caption: currently thinking a lot about how much less disabled I'd probably be if the general attitude in society to people – INCLUDING CHILDREN!!!! CHILDREN ARE PEOPLE!!!! – struggling or being slow or avoiding tasks would be to accomodate them and be patient, rather than to be annoyed or punish them. My earliest memories are of constantly getting chided for being slow. Sometimes it was good-naturedly, sometimes sternly, sometimes I was actually punished (slow at eating? not getting to eat my fill). At no single point did anyone wonder if I just needed more time than others and if this human variance, this diversity, might be tolerable. No, I had to be made to fit into the box, into the schedule. For no reason. Just 'cause. Was I already disabled or chronically ill as a kindergarten-aged child? Was that why I was slower than others, despite trying? It's possible. I don't know how I'd ever find out. But even without pathologising the way I have always been. I needed accommodations. And not getting them trained me to dissociate, to push myself past my limits on a daily basis as the default way to interact with anyone. It was fucking exhausting and everyone told me it wasn't. So I lost touch with my body's signals, distrusted them, actively faught them. A couple decades later my body is breaking down and no longer able to accommodate my rushing and pushing myself. I could compensate as a child, as a teenager. I stopped being able to in my 20s. I could still be part of society by living off benefits instead of having to work. Now, a few days before my 40s birthday, I can't take proper care of myself and can't even dream of participating in society beyond mastodon (and even then it's spotty). I deteriorated in a way that felt imperceptibly slow until it suddenly wasn't. And in hindsight, there was a steady progression. At no point did anyone (except Dion) consider encouraging me to slow down. To listen to my body and its limits. No. They all just assumed I needed to try harder, or that I'd always be miserable and pityable. It's not true though. I have turned the boat around, slowly. I am recovering now and am getting better. Slowly at first, I hope I will look back in a few decades and see as steady an incline from now on, as I had a decline before. Sure, I can't expect to be as spry as a 20yo when I'm 60, 70, 80. But I can be spry for my age. And I will get there by no longer trying so hard. By doing the actually hard work of allowing myself rest. # disability # DisabilityPrideMonth # ChronicIllness # ableism # AbuseCulture # adultism # AutisticBurnout # burnout

You can read the Community Tarot Reading for the Week here . Once I posted on Friday, I continued cleaning things up from my trip. Decontaminating anything that had been in the hotel room, making sure the car was decontaminated. Everything was probably fine, and I doubt anything traveled with me, but I wanted to make sure. I could barely keep my eyes open after I did the dishes, so I went to bed ridiculously early. The cats were confused. Slept reasonably well, in that I woke up a few times, but managed to get back to sleep without much trouble. It was a little uncomfortable when I went to bed, but cooled down overnight. I was up early on Saturday, due to the cats’ demands. Fed them, did my morning routine. The latest meditation timer dropped out because I haven’t upgraded to the paid version, so I hunted down another one to try free online (not an app). Meh. I used CSA ingredients for the greens, etc. I took out the garbage and did a quick trot on foot to the liquor store. It’s rosé season. I mean, the piece needs to wait its turn in the queue, but I can work on the background notes and outline between now and then. Historical literary fiction, imagine that. I’m sure a murder will sneak in at some point. One usually does. After lunch, I read some more, turned on the ceiling fan, and took the laptop into the living room. He trusts his jockey to tell him when to move up, they worked together as a team, and he did what he does, which is hang back (12 lengths from the lead this time), then pick off the horses in front of him one by one, and pass them as they wear out near the finish line. He actually pulled away pretty well at the end. The race was ¼ mile shorter than when it’s down at Belmont Park (where it will be again next year), so that was easier on all the horses. Still, it was impressive. Cherie DeVaux, the trainer, is the first woman trainer to win two of the three Triple Crown races in the same year. I got conflicting search results about who the first woman was to train a Belmont Stakes winner, and I no longer have as much thoroughbred history in my brain as I used to. Pere Antoine’s, my favorite restaurant in NOLA (alas, closed now) used to make a terrific Pain Perdu, and I’ve never been able to replicate it exactly. I was much closer this time. The recipe calls for 3 eggs mixed with ¾ cup of sugar. I add a teaspoon of vanilla. The bread is soaked in the mixture, flipped a few times to fully coat it, then fried in a buttered pan. The recipe calls for a sprinkling of nutmeg, but I found mixing nutmeg and cinnamon brings me closer to the recipe I’m trying to replicate. I got everything done except repotting the aloe, and it took all afternoon. But the plants are in their new homes, and happy. caption: I have lived through the earlier stages of life and now find myself in old age. At this stage, I no longer enjoy making tea or coffee alone at home. College students gather there in groups. From a distance, their bright laughter and lively chatter is a pleasure to watch and hear. Three such tea shops, near me, have closed down in the last few years. I used to go regularly to one particular tea and coffee shop. It was busier than the place I go to now. But the young people there smoked a lot. I did not like that. Sometimes I thought of telling them it was better not to smoke. I never found the courage to say it. The shop I visit now does not allow smoking. There is a Cafe Coffee Day near home. Earlier there were four such outlets. Now only one remains. It has two problems. The prices are very high. Older people come with their laptops. They are mostly serious and do not laugh. I have never seen college students there. At McDonald’s I do see groups of college boys and girls. Not at Cafe Coffee Day. That place seems meant for IT people. You cannot get tea or coffee there for twenty-five or thirty rupees. When I go to a tea and coffee shop, I consciously sit as far as I can from the college students. I cannot hear what they are saying. I simply enjoy the expressions on their faces and their smiles. caption: The bit that you skip 222: Blur – Sing Not gonna lie, the first days after arriving to Nottingham, solitude hit me like a tons of bricks. Perhaps all the walking and roaming around the campus and town was more to find some sort of solace, someone to converse with, to feel again. It’s a strange feeling, loneliness. I joined a few student societies, with varying results. Although I had sworn off religion, I somehow decided to join CathSoc too, and attend mass, something I hadn’t done willingly for more than a decade. I met a lot of interesting people and I remember one day chatting with some affable chaps about music and they both scowled when I mentioned “britpop”. They felt it was a bad term to use as it had been applied to bands willy nilly, pigeonholing some of them. Blur’s initial sound was the evolution of college rock, via sixth form and Madchester. A sort of crisper mix of baggy anthems and shoegaze. Dreamy, jangly atmospheres filtered to the eyes of straight rockers. Blur’s Leisure is The Smiths and The Stone Roses colliding. Modern Life is Rubbish was their make or break effort. The rivalry with Suede, which is often overlooked, seemed to hurt Blur’s reputation with the public much more than whatever schoolyard tiff they had with the Gallaghers. Thankfully Modern Life is Rubbish was their way out, possibly through the fierceness of Popscene, which lead into Parklife, the album that made them international stars. I liked The Great Escape just fine, but it’s their Be Here Now. Bloated, irregular, with immense heights and the lowest trenches. A well-trodden road was boring the public and the band. You understand why they distanced themselves. Blur had two choices: a steady decline or reinvent themselves. Oasis chose the former, Blur chose the latter. Their self-titled was as far as they could muster to throw themselves away to, and 13 was the opposite end of what Blur started as. No longer bumming cigs from friends. No more WKD drinks. Now wine, heroin, and rolled up ciggies. 13 is their swansong, the point where Blur 1.0 ceases to exist. Think thank is a Gorillaz demotape, too complicated for Blur fans, too light for Gorillaz fans. A funeral dirge that bricked Blur for almost 13 years before a factory reset. It was tough choosing one song, but Sing, for some reason or other, brings both joy and immense sadness to me. Pin it on its use on Trainspotting’s poignant scene. Pin it on being another Gen-Xer realising the best of their life is gone now and it’s all a long decline. -Sam J. Valdés López Nottingham blur depression Loneliness Sing Leisure
