caption: The Closed Door Trilogy: Part Two: The Bottom You Know When You Are There There is no dramatic announcement. No moment where the floor gives way and you fall through into something recognizably worse. The bottom just arrives. You realize you have been there for a few days already and did not mark the entry point. You look around at the interior of whatever this place is and understand, with a clarity that is almost clinical, that this is as far down as it goes. For him it looked like three days without leaving the apartment. It looked like food ordered because eating felt necessary and not because hunger had made itself known. It looked like the phone face-down on the table and the table existing at the far end of a room that felt very large. The Silence Gets Loud At the bottom, the silence stops being neutral. It accumulates. He could hear it in the way you hear a frequency that was always there but only becomes audible when everything else is gone. The absence of other people, of obligation, of performance, left him alone with a version of himself he did not particularly want to spend extended time with. He tried music once. Turned it off after four minutes. The gap between how it sounded and how he felt was too wide and the contrast made things worse. He tried television. Watched forty minutes of something he cannot now remember and turned it off because the people on screen seemed to be operating in a different physical reality, one where faces moved and mouths made sounds for reasons that felt alien and exhausting to track. What Nobody Sees Outside the door, life continued at its regular pace. He knew this in the abstract. People were having lunch and making plans and sending messages he was not answering and probably, some of them, wondering if they had done something wrong. He felt bad about that in the part of himself that was still capable of feeling bad about things. The part had gotten smaller. He cried once, on the second day. Not with any particular trigger. Just the accumulated pressure of everything finding its only available exit. He sat on the bathroom floor because that is where it happened, and he let it run its course, and then he washed his face with cold water and looked at himself in the mirror for a long time without thinking anything in particular, and then he went back to the room and the silence and the phone face-down on the table. The Knock on the Third Day He did not answer it. But he heard it. And then he heard a voice through the door, not asking to be let in, not demanding an explanation, just saying his name and then saying: I am going to leave something here. You do not have to open the door. I just wanted you to know I came. He sat very still on the other side of the door and listened to the footsteps move away down the hall. He did not open the door for another hour. When he did, there was food and a note that said nothing except: still here when you are ready. He stood in the doorway and looked at the empty hallway for a long time. He did not feel better. But he felt something shift, some small tectonic thing deep underneath the weight, that was not better exactly but was different from what it had been five minutes before. The Bottom Is Not the End That is what he learned on the third day, not as an insight or a revelation, just as a fact he had gathered enough evidence to provisionally accept. The bottom has a floor. It is not bottomless. You hit it and it holds you, not comfortably, not warmly, but structurally. It does not let you through. He ate the food. He read the note twice. He did not text back that night. But he kept the note. fictionSeries healingAlone Loneliness mentalHealth shortStorySeries silentSuffering socialMedia theClosedDoorTrilogy ZsoltZsemba

caption: The Closed Door Trilogy: Part One: The Descent It Starts Before You Notice It Starting It never arrives all at once. That is the thing nobody tells you. It does not show up at the door with its name on a sign. It seeps in. A Tuesday that feels heavier than it should. A conversation that leaves you emptier than before it happened. A moment where you look at the life around you and feel nothing that resembles ownership of it. You notice you have stopped laughing at things that used to be funny. You notice the bed feels like the only honest place in the room. By the time you realize what is happening, it has already been happening for a while. The Door Closes Quietly He did not make a decision to pull back. It just happened the way erosion happens. Gradually, then completely. First, he stopped returning calls he would have returned before. Then he started leaving messages on read without the guilt that used to follow. Then the invitations stopped feeling like opportunities and started feeling like obligations he did not have the resources to meet. He told himself it was temporary. He told himself he just needed a few days to reset, to find his footing, to get back to some version of himself that felt inhabitable. He believed it the first few times he said it. By the third week, he had stopped keeping count. What the Darkness Actually Feels Like People use darkness as a metaphor, and it is not wrong, but it is incomplete. It is not just the absence of light. It is the presence of weight. Everything costs more than it should. Getting up costs something. Eating costs something. Responding to a simple question from someone who genuinely cares costs something he does not always have on hand. He moves through the hours like a man walking against a current that nobody else in the room can feel. He does not talk about it. Not because there are no words. There are too many words, and none of them land anywhere useful. He has tried before. He has watched the face of someone listening arrange itself into concern and felt the distance between what he was trying to say and what they were able to receive, and decided the gap was not worth crossing. The Worst Nights Have a Particular Quality They are quieter than the others. Not peaceful and quiet. The kind of quiet that has texture. He lies in the dark, and the thoughts are not dramatic, which somehow makes them worse. They are just steady and low and certain in the way that exhausted things are certain. He does not spiral. He just sinks. Slowly, without theatrics, into something he cannot quite name but recognizes by now. He knows people are out there. He can picture them, specific faces, people who would pick up on the first ring. He does not reach for the phone. Not because he does not want a connection. Because want requires energy, he is running too low to access. He Will Not Tell You How Close It Gets Not tonight. Maybe not ever. There are edges in those nights that he does not revisit in daylight, not because they were not real, but because bringing them back into the light feels like giving them more oxygen than they deserve. What he will tell you is that the night always ends. Not cleanly. Not with resolution. Just with the particular gray that comes before morning, the colour of something that has not decided yet what it is going to be. He makes it to the gray every time. He has not yet decided if that is a strength or just the stubbornness of a body that keeps going before the mind has agreed to. Either way, he is still here at the start of the next day. caption: Thousands of Followers and Nearly Completely Alone? We Built the Most Connected World in History and Somehow Got Lonelier Somewhere between the first social media account and the ten thousandth follower, something shifted. Not dramatically. Not all at once. Just quietly, the way the most important changes tend to happen. We started measuring our social lives in metrics. Reach. Engagement. Impressions. We started performing connections instead of having it. And we got so good at the performance that most of us stopped noticing the difference. The numbers went up. The loneliness went up with them. That is not a coincidence. What the Research Actually Says The evidence on social media and mental health has been building for years, and it is not ambiguous. Studies consistently show that heavy social media use is associated with higher rates of anxiety, depression, and loneliness across all age groups, with the sharpest effects in adolescents and young adults. A 2023 report from the US Surgeon General identified social media as a significant contributing factor to the youth mental health crisis, noting that adolescents who spend more than three hours a day on social platforms face double the risk of depression and anxiety symptoms. The comparison effect is relentless. Every scroll is a highlight reel from someone else’s life positioned against the unedited reality of your own. The brain was not built to process that volume of social comparison. For most of human history, you compared yourself to maybe a few dozen people you actually knew. Now you compare yourself to thousands of curated strangers before breakfast. The AI Problem Nobody Is Talking About Loudly Enough And then there is AI. Tools like the one generating this post. Conversational, available around the clock, endlessly patient, never tired, never distracted, never having a bad day that bleeds into how it treats you. It is easy to see why people find that appealing. It is also worth being honest about what it costs. When you can have a conversation with an AI instead of texting a friend, you remove the friction of a human relationship. The vulnerability. The reciprocity. The fact that the other person has their own needs, bad days and limits. That friction is not a flaw in human connection. It is the mechanism by which genuine intimacy is built. Remove it, and you get something that feels like connection but does not do what connection actually does for a human nervous system. AI does not replace human connection. It displaces the impulse to seek it. And that is a different and more subtle kind of damage. Thousands of Followers and a Silent Phone There is a specific kind of loneliness that belongs to the social media age, and it does not have a clean name yet. It is the loneliness of someone whose content reaches ten thousand people and who has nobody to call when something goes wrong. The loneliness of being publicly visible and privately invisible. The loneliness of a comment section full of strangers and a contact list full of people you have not spoken to in months because the algorithm convinced you that posting was the same as connecting. It is not. Posting is broadcasting. Connection requires two people actually showing up for each other, imperfectly, in real time, with something genuinely at stake. The Mental Health Crisis Nobody Wants to Fully Acknowledge Rates of depression, anxiety, and suicide have climbed steadily in the years since smartphones became ubiquitous. The World Health Organization estimates that more than 700,000 people die by suicide each year globally, making it one of the leading causes of death among people aged 15 to 29. That number existed before social media. But the platforms have added new dimensions to the problem: cyberbullying, social exclusion that happens publicly and permanently, the pressure to perform wellness while privately deteriorating, and the algorithmic amplification of content that keeps distressed people in loops of distressing material. The person posting daily about their perfect life may be falling apart privately. The person who has gone quiet on their feed may be going dark in the way that actually matters. The metrics tell you nothing about what is actually happening inside the person generating them. What to Do If You Are the Person Behind the Closed Door If any of this is landing somewhere personal, that matters more than anything else in this post. The research on social isolation and mental health is clear: connection with other humans, a real connection, is one of the most protective factors against depression and suicidal thinking. Not followers. Not likes. Not an AI that is available at 3 am. Actual people who know you and show up. If you are struggling and not reaching out because you do not want to be a burden, consider this: the people who care about you would rather be burdened than uninformed. And if there is nobody in your immediate life you feel you can reach, there are people whose entire purpose is to be there for exactly that moment. Indonesia: Into The Light at 119 International: The International Association for Suicide Prevention maintains a directory of crisis centers at Global: The WHO mental health resources are available at The Algorithm Is Not Your Friend. But You Probably Have Some. Log off for an hour. Text someone you have not spoken to in a while. Have a conversation that cannot be liked, shared or measured in any way. Let it be awkward, imperfect, and human. That is not a step backward from modern life. It is the thing modern life keeps trying to replace with something that looks similar but does not actually work. You have followers. Go find your people. caption: # neuroscience # loneliness # dopamine # SocialInteraction "Why we crave company Neuroscientists are discovering that spending time with others may be a basic biological necessity, like need for food or water. To our human eyes, a mouse’s furred face doesn’t betray much emotion. But if you watch the body language of a mouse who’s reunited with one of her sisters after five days in a cage alone, you might suspect you know what she’s feeling. The formerly isolated mouse chatters in squeaks too high for a human to hear. She follows her sister, crawling beneath the other mouse’s body as if trying to get a hug. She looks like she’s feeling what you or I feel when meeting a long-lost friend or a family member — maybe with more sniffing. She looks like she’s been lonely. Loneliness isn’t just for humans, and neither are its harms. Over the past decade or so, some researchers have come to believe that an animal’s craving for the company of others isn’t just a preference, but a basic, deeply held need. When we don’t socialize enough, we feel the lack like hunger or thirst, they say. When we’ve had our fill of togetherness, we feel satisfied or quenched. The amount of socializing a creature needs may be particular to that species, and even to that individual. Scientists have found within-species social differences in birds, monkeys, fish and even cockroaches. Among humans, 'you can feel lonely at a party, or you can feel fine alone in your office,' says Kay Tye, a neuroscientist at the Salk Institute for Biological Studies in California. Whatever the ideal degree of togetherness, Tye and others think that an animal’s need to balance time alone and time with others represents a kind of homeostasis: an equilibrium that’s critical for survival. Today, they are on a hunt to find where, in the brain, this equilibrium is controlled — and hoping their work will hold dividends for lonely humans. (. . .) Within each species, Clutton-Brock says evolution has probably allowed for a range of personality types around a certain species average. 'There are costs to too much anxiety' about being alone, he says, 'and costs to too little anxiety.' A species may do best with a mix of social styles. Whatever an animal’s right amount of social activity, research suggests there can be dire consequences to mental and physical health when it’s not met. People who are socially isolated, or feel lonely, die sooner. Poor social connections are linked to heart disease and stroke. Certain female rats, when housed alone, are more likely to develop cancer. (. . .) The scientists hypothesized that other animals, including humans, share this system. Though it’s not easy to test such a thing in people, Tye did team up with a research group at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology for an experiment in which people sat alone in a room for 10 hours. Afterward, subjects reported craving social interaction. When they viewed pictures of people laughing together, their brains lit up in the same region as the brains of fasting subjects who viewed pictures of food: an area, also within the brainstem, packed with dopamine neurons that are involved in cravings. (. . .) What’s more, when scientists used a technical trick called optogenetics to artificially activate the separation neurons every time the animals entered a certain chamber, the mice avoided spending time there. That suggested that these brain cells, when activated, give the mice a bad feeling. 'It’s unpleasant to be alone, in the same way it has been shown that it’s unpleasant to be hungry,' says Dulac, who coauthored an overview of social interaction as a fundamental need in the 2026 Annual Review of Neuroscience." https:// knowablemagazine.org/content/a rticle/mind/2026/why-we-crave-social-interaction

caption: Marriage Won’t Fix Your Loneliness There’s a version of loneliness that nobody talks about honestly. Not the kind that hits you on a Friday night when your phone isn’t buzzing. The deeper kind. The kind that follows you into a full house, a shared bed, a family dinner table. The kind that makes you wonder why, with all these people around, you still feel completely alone. Most men don’t sit with that question long enough to answer it. They solve it instead. They find a woman, build something with her, have kids, chase a bigger salary, fill the calendar. For a while, it works, or it feels like it works. Then one day the noise dies down, and there it is again. Same heaviness. Same hollow feeling. Waiting. That’s because loneliness isn’t a situation. It’s a symptom. What You’re Actually Running From The problem isn’t that you’re single, or broke, or sexually frustrated. Those things might be true, and they’re worth addressing on their own terms. But the loneliness underneath all of that isn’t going away because your circumstances improved. It goes away when you look at what’s actually driving it. For most men, that loneliness traces back to something specific. A version of themselves they abandoned at some point. The kid who was told to stop being so sensitive. The teenager who learned that vulnerability gets punished. The adult who built walls so convincing that he forgot they were walls. He walks through life making connections without actually making them. He builds a family and realizes he doesn’t know how to let them in. Marriage doesn’t fix that. It exposes it. Why the Big Moves Don’t Work There’s a reason so many men arrive at forty with everything they thought they wanted and still feel like something is missing. The house, the kids, the career, the relationship. All checked. And yet. The problem is the logic of acquisition. We are raised to believe that the right external circumstances will produce the right internal state. Get the girl, feel worthy. Make the money, feel secure. Start a family, feel complete. This is how most men operate for the better part of their lives, and it produces results that look great in photos and feel hollow in private. Sex doesn’t fix loneliness either. It can mask it for an hour. A good night with someone you care about can make you feel close, connected, and seen. But if you’re using sex to feel less alone, you already know how fast that wears off. You already know the feeling of lying next to someone and still being completely inside your own head. None of these things is wrong to want. The problem is expecting them to do a job they were never designed to do. The Only Thing That Actually Works Coming to terms with your issues is not a therapy cliche. It’s the unsexy, uncomfortable, non-negotiable work of actually understanding yourself. Why do you respond the way you do? What you’re afraid of. What you’ve been carrying since before you had the language for it. What you keep recreating in every relationship because you never dealt with it the first time. This is where most men tap out. It’s easier to find a new woman than to face why the last three relationships followed the same pattern. Easier to work longer hours than to sit with the discomfort of not knowing who you are outside of productivity. Easier to have another drink, plan another trip, start another project. The men who do the work stop feeling as lonely. Not because their circumstances became perfect, but because they stopped being strangers to themselves. When you actually know who you are, a real connection becomes possible. Not the performance of it. This Isn’t About Going It Alone None of this means marriage is pointless or that kids won’t add something real to your life. It means the sequence matters. If you bring an unexamined version of yourself into a relationship, you bring your unresolved loneliness with you. The other person becomes responsible for fixing something they didn’t break and can’t reach. The men who build something genuinely good with another person tend to be the ones who have spent real time understanding themselves first. Not perfectly. Not with every issue resolved. But with enough self-awareness to stop outsourcing their emotional life to whoever is standing closest. You can get married. You can have kids. You can make a lot of money and have a very active sex life. All of that is available to you. But if you skip the part where you actually deal with yourself, you will feel alone in every single one of those situations. That’s not a warning. It’s just what happens. alone emptiness familyAndFriends friends frustrated Loneliness marriage partners ZsoltZsemba

caption: If You Don’t Know Who You Are Alone, Relationships Will Confuse the Hell Out of You Nobody tells you this when you’re young. You spend your whole adolescence being shaped by what other people think of you, what your parents wanted you to become, and what the culture tells you success looks like. You absorb all of it. You build a personality around it. And then one day you find yourself in a relationship, wondering why you feel so lost, why you keep reacting in ways you don’t fully understand, why the person across from you seems to trigger something you can’t quite name. The answer is usually the same. You never figured out who you are when nobody is watching. Most men walk into relationships as a work in progress; they haven’t started yet. They know their job title, their taste in music, and their football team. They don’t know their patterns. They don’t know what they actually need versus what they think they’re supposed to want. They don’t know where they end, and other people begin. So when a relationship puts pressure on all of that, the confusion is total. The Mirror Problem Relationships have a way of reflecting things back at you. A partner who pulls away makes you realize you have an abandonment wound you never addressed. A partner who criticizes you activates something from childhood you thought you’d outgrown. A partner who needs too much space makes you question your own worth in ways that have nothing to do with them. None of this is their fault. The mirror doesn’t create what it shows you. It just shows you. The problem is that most men haven’t done the work to understand what they’re looking at when it appears. So instead of recognizing the reflection, they blame the mirror. They blame her for being distant, critical, or suffocating. They end the relationship. They find a new one. The same patterns show up again within six months, wearing a different face. This is not bad luck. This is what happens when you enter a relationship without knowing yourself. What You Think You Want vs. What You Actually Need Here’s where it gets complicated. A man who doesn’t know himself doesn’t know the difference between what he wants and what he needs. He thinks he wants a woman who doesn’t challenge him. What he needs is someone who makes him feel safe enough to be honest. He thinks he wants constant closeness. What he needs is to learn that he can be alone without falling apart. He thinks he wants someone to fix the emptiness. What he needs is to stop outsourcing that job. This gap between want and need is where most relationships quietly die. Two people who both don’t know themselves, trying to fill in the blanks with each other, eventually realizing the blanks are still there and blaming each other for it. You cannot bridge that gap from inside a relationship. You can do some of the work there, if you’re lucky and both people are willing. But the foundation has to be laid before you walk in. Alone Is the Practice Ground Being alone is not a waiting room. It’s not the unpleasant gap between relationships that you have to survive until the next one starts. It’s the only place where you can actually hear yourself think without someone else’s needs, expectations, or projections filling up the space. When you’re alone, and you sit with that discomfort instead of immediately solving it, you learn something. You learn what actually bothers you versus what you can let go. You learn how you talk to yourself when nobody is listening. You learn whether you actually like your own company, and if you don’t, that tells you something important. The men who figure out who they are when they’re alone tend to show up differently in relationships. Not perfectly. Not without issues. But with enough self-knowledge to stop reacting blindly, to take some responsibility for their patterns, to ask for what they need instead of punishing a partner for not reading their mind. The Real Cost of Skipping This Skipping the work of knowing yourself doesn’t just hurt you. It hurts whoever you’re with. You become unpredictable to them because you’re unpredictable to yourself. You make them responsible for your emotional stability. You confuse love with need and then resent them when they can’t meet all of it. The relationships that actually work, the ones that hold up under pressure and still feel like something good years later, are almost always built by people who came in with some degree of self-knowledge. Not perfect self-knowledge. Just enough to know where they were standing. You can start a relationship without knowing yourself. Plenty of people do. But at some point, the confusion becomes impossible to ignore. The question is whether you address it before it costs you something you actually care about. caption: Does the male loneliness epidemic really exist? Throughout history, even in the beliefs they fabricated, men found a way to unite. They supported each other or challenged each other, somehow remaining connected. They clinked glasses in pubs, or smashed bottles over each other's heads. They womanized together, committed crimes together, debated ideas, collectively pacified others (regardless of their gender), understood each other with just a glance. They flattered each other, shared their feelings in the limited ways they knew. They left their families to gamble in casinos, supported each other on the front lines of the wars they themselves started, formed brotherhood bonds with their army buddies, writing a magnificent history of brotherhood. Men were always together. They slept together, had sex with each other without anyone knowing, they fought each other and then made peace, like brothers who fought and then hugged in the playground, but never truly separated. Does this make masculinity a bit like the biggest single-cell organism in history? Or is there a collective delusion to deflect blame? Just pause for a second, And think. Maybe it's not loneliness. Maybe it's just the personal and painful realisation that one is simply an ordinary human being. "Why wasn't I declared the most special, the most powerful, the alpha, the king, as I hoped? Why wasn't I made to feel 'most privileged' by everyone? Why do I have to strive for money, education, status, sex? Why do I have to work hard for respect? Why isn't masculinity alone enough to make others carry me on their shoulders" Maybe penis is not a divine sceptre, no matter how much the world wants you to believe in that. Embracing your humanity, instead of obsessing about a mythical, unachievable maleness, might be a solution. Memento mori. # masculinity # philosophy # psychology # mentalhealth # loneliness

caption: The Original Wound: Storymere Excerpt Photo by Nate Biddle on Pexels.com This is a hard chapter to read. I’ve spent most of the day in tears over it (5,299 words written today; this shows you how deeply I was in it). It is the original wound for Storymere (that takes you to more detail about the story’s concept; this takes you to another excerpt). This story is one I care very deeply about. I hope you come to love these characters as much as I do. Ultimately, the novel traces this family over the course of 100 years. I wake while it is still night. I know it’s too early to rise because the shape of Neene still lies on her mat, her body turned toward us. The room is grey and still and quiet except for Awa. She breathes with her mouth parted, as though she can’t be quiet even when she’s asleep. Something scratches outside. One of the village dogs or a curious goat looks for scraps. When I roll, I notice Baaba’s sleeping place is empty; his mat, rolled up neatly, leans against the woven wall. Frowning, I sit, yawning. There’s no sense in letting daylight waste away. Neene says this when she catches Awa sitting still instead of finding something useful to do. Neene would smile at me, pat my back, and tell me thank you if some of the chores are done before Fajr. I stand silently, smiling when a sliver of moonlight reveals a speck of dust on Awa’s chin. She just can’t help herself: dirt gathers around her like bees to honey. I hesitate but choose my pretty blue wrapper to wear. When I pull the nightshift off, gooseflesh rises along the thin, soft hairs of my legs. I haven’t worn the pretty blue wrapper since Neene and Baaba gave it to me; it still feels stiff as it drapes around me, its ends brushing lightly against my ankles. When I step outside, I look up first. The sky still holds the stars; they twinkle above me. Since I’ll have to wash my feet for Fajr anyway, I don’t wear my sandals. The gritty, tawny dirt beneath my soles feels like home. The thought makes me look beyond the hills toward the river and Samba’s settlement. “Do ya think that’s enoug’?” Sometimes his words curl around each other, the beginnings and endings blurring. “Do you think that’s enough for a hearth?” I ask as we stare into the small brown box where a handful of Djéol dirt now lies. “You add some.” Small pebbles and bits of loose rock and dirt harden the ground; a jagged crack formed by the dry season’s relentless sun snags the corner of my gaze. I work to loosen the dirt until it crumbles; using the side of one hand, I scoop some into my other palm. The whispering sound of it sliding into the box and onto the dirt he’s already collected sounds almost like a promise. Samba’s face changes; his smile grows. “That’s enough gold.” Feeding the poultry is Awa’s morning chore, but when I see the coarse-woven sack lying on its side, its mouth open and a light dusting of millet spilt onto the ground, I shake my head. She left the millet out and some animal got into it . A few tiny tracks near the sack confirm a mouse found an easy supper. Bending down, I scoop the excess millet into my palm and toss it over the pen for the chickens. Soon, I’ve cleaned the ground, fed them and returned the tied sack to storage. The mouse will have to look elsewhere for food tonight. The sound of a donkey braying turns my head. Baaba. The donkey’s ears twitch as he stops near the hut. Neene comes out, calls hello and walks toward the earthen wall. Baaba dismounts, checks the sky. Fajr nears. “Isn’t that your sister’s task?” he asks, his brows arched. I shrug. “There was time to do it now.” “Everything alright?” Neene asks, coming back, glancing at the horizon. Baaba nods. “Bocar and I went; we didn’t see anything around the boundary.” Taking the rope tied around the donkey’s neck, Baaba walks toward the tethering post. Neene’s shoulders loosen. “Good. I’ll start the water.” The air in the hut feels different when I step back inside; alive instead of asleep. Except for Awa. She still lies with her eyes closed and her mouth open, her breathing slow and steady. Reaching down, I shake her arm. She frowns, her lips closing, and rolls away from me. “Come on, Awa. It’s time for wudu and prayer.” I shake her again. When she doesn’t open her eyes, I coil my pinkie around a fuzzy curl and give two quick tugs. She moans, her hand reaching out to slap my arm. “Stop,” she moans. “Get up.” Her mouth stretches wide, yawning, and one honey-brown eye opens. I smile. “Good morning, Awa.” Still groggy, she sits. “I’m going to the wall.” I follow her outside. As she goes to relieve herself, I look for the water Neene has prepared. The bowl is wide and the water swirls. Crouching down, I pour it into my hands. Rivulets of clear liquid trickle through my fingers as I rub my skin. By the time I’ve washed my face, Awa stands beside me, still in her nightshift. She pours too much over her hands and it spills, darkening a patch of earth. After completing the washing of my face and head, I rub the dirt and pebbles from my feet and ankles and then slip my toes into my sandals. I move around the hut to stand facing Mecca. I am the first in position. A dog barks once from somewhere close. Beyond the bark, there’s another sound but I can’t make out what it is. It’s still dark; moonlight reveals nothing. When the dog’s barking becomes louder and incessant, something uneasy blooms in my belly. My heart pounds: it is loud. There it is again—someone shouting. Something’s not right. Then— Horses. Not one. Many. Suddenly, a very loud, very clear shout: “Hasani!” Noise bursts. I turn, looking for Awa. “Baaba—” The shouts grow even louder. I see Mammadu and Uncle run into view; their faces scare me. “Oumar!” “Get with your mother now !” I’ve never heard Baaba’s voice sound like that. He runs past me, calling for Mammadu: “Follow the plan; women and children to the river!” “Aïssata!” Neene screams from the door of the hut. She has Awa’s wrist in her hand and runs at me, grabbing mine. The shouts turn to screams. “ River!” Baaba yells at Neene as he and the men run from the house. Neene hesitates, her eyes wild and wide. She spins, looking south toward the river, gauging. “Neene?” Awa cries, tugging our mother’s arm. “I don’t know, I don’t know…” Neene whispers and panic floods her face. Women scatter; some head toward the river, others into abandoned huts. Neene freezes, swallowing repeatedly. Without warning, a dozen horses, taller than the sky, swarm into the middle of our settlement. It’s their presence that makes Neene run, dragging us behind her. Men with flowing robes and cloth around their heads scream from the saddles; they swing long blades. Some have crackling torches. Suddenly, a loud blast pierces the dawn. I don’t see where it comes from but the ringing in my ears makes me scream. Awa pulls her hands up to cover her ears; Neene doesn’t let her wrist go even as the sound stops us cold. Smoke spreads everywhere; the donkey breaks its tether and runs; Mammadu moves to strike, lifting a blade. Someone behind him makes the loud blast again; I am coughing when I see Mammadu fall. The ground doesn’t look gold anymore; it looks red. Awa screams for Baaba. There are people everywhere. Fear courses through my veins. We round Uncle’s hut. Men scream in our faces; Neene lets go of my wrist, grabs my chin so I look into her eyes and screams, “Run!” The word doesn’t make sense to me. What does it mean? Before I can move, a man, thick-shouldered, with wild eyes and a gleaming lance, grabs me by my arm. Awa wails my name. Someone yanks her from Neene; I can’t see his face. Neene’s shrill howl is the loudest thing I’ve ever heard, even louder than the shots fired. Awa flails, squatting, pulling against the arms that hold her, and ends on the ground, on her back, one arm over her head as he drags her. Something in my chest unravels. I scramble, trying to reach the hand she’s holding out toward me. “Aïssata!” She looks so small still in her nightshift and I stretch, reaching as far as I can toward her. Our fingers brush but are not close enough to grasp. As I’m pulled further away from my sister, my fingernail bites deep into my skin. The noise around me garbles. All I hear is Awa, but I can’t see her anymore. People move between us. My chest tightens; bubbles rise into my throat and I can’t breathe. I stumble because we’re moving too quick. I fall and my eyes land on the edge of my blue wrapper. The shouting, the tightness of the man’s fingers around my arm, Neene calling my name—everything fades. The rim of my wrapper grows, as though billowed by the wind, and I’m not sure now if the blue is my wrapper or the sky. The color swirls, moving from the deep blue of the garment to the washed azure of a cloudless sky. A river rushes beside me. The clear water babbles over stones the shade of powdered chalk and flows toward the sea. Thin reeds crowd its banks. Birds sit high on branches of acacias. When I look into the water, I notice one such branch, but it doesn’t look like any branch; it is ripe with colors. A tiny sunbird with iridescent green and blue feathers sings loudly while two red-cheeked cordon-bleu finches survey the river from one branch higher. They’re playing with paints! Awa says this whenever she sees one. Through the river’s mirror, I notice the leaves, too. One looks smaller than the others; it quivers. Or maybe it sways? Or maybe it’s the river’s current playing tricks? Its color is more vibrant than leaves usually are. It shimmers like emerald but sometimes, when the light falls, it looks more like a parakeet’s wing. The reflection is so clear I see a strong ridge, a vein, that runs down its center and branches off into smaller lines. At the end of the vein, the leaf’s tip is pointed and there are tiny, jagged edges down its sides. I stare at the fuzzy tips, wondering if they’re sharp. From somewhere far, a sound with a familiar, yet oddly different, shape makes me look. Suddenly, droplets of water land on my foot as something breaches the river’s surface. Too quickly for me to see what it was, I lean back and move to swipe the wetness from my toes. But it isn’t river spray. It’s dark red, darker than the cordon-bleu’s red cheeks, splattered over me. Someone jostles my shoulder just as a gunshot shakes the earth. I hear whimpering as Awa only does when she’s scared. My eyes grow wild; where is she? “Awa! Neene!” I scream as people crowd around me. “Aïssata. I’m here. We’re here. Stay with me.” Neene bursts forth from behind me. Her breath is shallow and she drags one leg. Blood? Why is she bleeding? Awa. She takes my hand and I squeeze it. The small, constant hm hm hm whine breaks up her breathing. Crowded between the horses and men, I strain my neck to see. “Where’s Baaba?” My voice hitches. A man in grey and brown flowing robes appears in front of us. He jerks my hands first, ties them together at the wrists with a rope that he then uses to bind Awa and Neene. We’re forced back into a line; Awa stands between us. I stand behind Takko who wails hysterically until one of the men screams in her face that she will lose her head if she doesn’t get quiet. The screaming stops, but the crying does not. Swoosh . Orange flames devour a few of our huts. The smell of smoke and ash and sweat and blood makes me wish I was beside Neene instead of in front of her. Our cattle—some of them are being herded with us, others lie on the ground. Bodies, too. Bodies lie on the ground; they don’t move. I jerk my eyes away from them. The hooves of the horse beside me step on a striped mat and tears spill down my cheeks, my eyes moving to the sky. We can’t do Fajr. I count steps. Eleven, twelve— a man on horseback chuckles. Twelve steps this time before someone laughs. I start over. One, two, three… A small body pushes me forward: Awa. I catch myself before falling into Takko, glancing behind my shoulder. Awa’s legs tremble. Neene reaches out, puts a hand on her shoulder, steadying her. We’ve walked for hours. We missed Dhuhr, stopping only for the men to tend to the animals. Squinting, I check the sky. It’s hazy with dust from the march and the horses. The paleness of the sky makes me wonder if it tires as we do. My shadow stretches to the east, longer than it has. Shadows are dark, black like midnight. “ I talk to mine. Do you talk to your shadow, Samba?” He smiles. “What do you talk to yours about?” I shrug, skipping a stone across the surface of the river. “Anything I want. Sometimes I sing to it.” This delights him. His whole face changes, as though he’s tasted something sweet. “Do you?” “Praise to Allah, who brings light with the MORning Who lifts the dark and OPENS our eyes—” “Does your shadow dance with you?” I giggle. “Maybe it can.” “Let’s try it.” And so we learn: shadows can dance. Seven, eight— a loud bark of laughter. Eight steps. A man’s voice from up ahead says something. Horses stop. My back straightens. “Neene?” Awa asks quietly. “Shh, it’s alright.” A few stay on their horses, watching us. Some pull grain for the horses to munch. But I notice a few turn to Mecca. I frown, turn. “Neene,” I whisper. “Look.” Murmurs; bows; kneels. “Asr,” Neene whispers. “I want to pray.” Neene’s lips open, close. She blinks back tears. “I know.” The rope around my wrist feels tighter than before. I watch as the men repeat the steps of Asr. It pulls the rope when I follow to the ground, but I do it anyway. I can’t spread my hands as I normally do, but I try. My lips move with the words to the prayer, not sure if I have the timing or not. Awa watches me but presses back against Neene. My heart squeezes until it hurts because it doesn’t feel the same. Maybe that’s why Neene stands still. When I look back at Neene, she tries to smile at me and her lip trembles as she whispers, “Well done, Aïssata.” Well done, Aïssata. I repeat it again, trying to make her voice louder. Well done, Aïssata. “Why do they pray?” I ask, watching the men in robes. As they finish Asr, the noise picks up again; someone shouts. Men mount. In my head, I tell Samba, “Shadows pray, too.” There is noise around us, but all we hear is the quiet. The stars are out, and the men have crowded us together beneath trees. Men gather around crackling fires. Their guns and lances are always with them. One of the villagers, though bound, nurses a little one. Awa rocks back and forth, picking at a scab on her foot. Neene stares at the cut on her leg, swollen from walking, with dried blood trailing down to her ankle, but does nothing about it. Every now and then, she closes her eyes slowly and her lips move, though nothing comes out. I hear Neene’s voice, but I don’t know what she says. Words are confusing now. She reaches her wrists out to tip the small bowl they gave each of us toward me. The soup sloshes to the side. I stare straight ahead. I don’t feel anything else. My heart doesn’t race. I can breathe, although it’s different now. A star catches my attention. It pulses like the drum against my skull. “Aïssata.” I blink, my eyes moving toward my mother. “Look at me.” My gaze lifts to her face. Something shifts in her face, loosens, when I meet her eyes. She gripped my chin hard. “Run!” She nods, pats my knee. I didn’t run. My eyes slink away from hers. “Where’s Baaba?” Awa asks quietly, still rocking. “I think I saw him fall,” Takko’s mother, Binta, says. “No, I saw him on the way out,” Rokhaya differs. Neene straightens. “Where?” “It might not have been him. Was he on horseback or donkey?” Rokhaya asks. “Donkey.” Neene hesitates. “I think.” “I think the one I saw was on horseback. But… but I’m not sure.” “Did anyone see anyone from the river settlement? Bocar or Samba?” Binta asks. Samba. My heart skips a beat and then pounds hard. No one remembers seeing them. I didn’t look for him. Tears well. I pull my knees to my chest and hide my face. Allah wants us to help our friends. I am certain next time you will find a way to do both. But I didn’t, Baaba. I didn’t. With my head tucked into my knees, my breath becomes loud, like a whisper that wants to be more than a whisper. Neene asks Awa if she’s cold, tells her to scoot closer to her and lean against her. “I want Baaba.” Awa’s voice is quiet and trembles like my heart. My chin touches my chest and, in the darkness, I see the outline of the pendant. I pull the cord with blue and white beads from over my head and palm the copper. My thumb rubs over the eight-pointed star, and then over the broken arm. That one is broken. That one is copper. I tilt it so the moonlight catches it; the silver beam makes the metal look almost like amber. I look at Awa. “Look up,” I say quietly. Awa tips her head back. Neene raises her head, too. We stare at the sky and its pulsing stars. “There was a girl whose father traveled very far.” I swallow. “She was scared because she thought he might be swallowed by the distance. It was very far that he had to go.” “Where?” Awa asks. The moon is pale but I know she wants me to tell her where he is. Bubbles stick in my throat. I look down at the pendant, rub the broken arm. “Far. But every night she would pick a hoodere. Any would do.” “Which one do you pick?” Awa asks, watching the twinkling lights. “I like that one,” Neene joins, tugging the rope so she can point to a star just above us. Awa thinks for a moment and chooses one beside Neene’s. I say, “The girl always picked the first bright one she could find. Her father would say it didn’t matter where the road went. He would look for a star too. Every night he was away.” “But he was far.” “It didn’t matter. The girl thought there were two skies. One for her and one for him. She thought maybe the stars chose which sky they wanted and maybe they didn’t always pick the same one.” Baaba pulls a slip of copper from his garment, turns it between large fingers. “The star never chose.” I repeat it now: “The stars never choose because there was never one sky for him and one sky for her. There was only one sky.” I slip the pendant back around my neck. I swallow, singing the words to the song Awa wrote, “When I cannot see your face, I will lift my eyes.” Neene smiles. “That’s the melody to our morning song.” I lean over, nudging my sister’s shoulder, forcing my lips to tilt. “What does Allah bring in the morning?” It takes Awa time. I don’t think she’s going to answer. Maybe she don’t remember. Maybe she can’t. But then her shoulders shake and she moves, lying her head in my lap. “Millet,” she whispers, wiping her nose with the back of her hand. The sun blisters. The horse swats his tail. A fly buzzes near my nose; I jerk my head away. From behind us, cattle low. Leather squeaks as the men shift in the saddles. The gold dirt turns more ochre and is firmer than at home. There aren’t as many acacia trees and we pass a few stones. Awa slows by the time the pinks and purples brush against the golden rays of the sun. Without warning, a man in flowing robes and a brown headwrap tells us to stop. Across his chest, a large gun sways. When he grabs Awa’s wrists, Neene cries out, “No, please—” He removes the rope and thrusts my sister up to the Hassane riding beside us. “Neene!” Awa cries, trying to reach down. The man holding her speaks low. I can’t hear what he says but Awa stops talking. I can see her shaking from here. “Walk,” the man orders, shoving my shoulder. I feel Neene crowding against my back. She whispers, “Faster, Aïssata.” My own feet and ankles are swollen but I move as quick as I can, crowding against Takko’s back, until I feel the rope that connects us all shift to the side. Neene’s dark fingers grasp Awa’s heel. She doesn’t let go. When Awa turns her head to look down, I hear Neene say, “We’re right here. We’re right beside you.” And we walk. The sun moves slowly. Sweat collects on my upper lip and along my forehead. When the men drink, I track the gourd. We are too hot and too tired to talk. I walk and stare at the horizon where the lines are wavy because that feels like my insides. Blurry. I feel the shift before I know why. The men hurry us; donkeys and horses are spurred into quick trots. Voices start talking over one another. And then, in the distance, I see them. Tents. Still holding Awa’s heel, Neene breathes in, fast and shallow. My eyes widen. As we get closer, we see men and women walking from tent to tent. Market , I think. The rope pulls against my wrist. Skin peels; blisters rise. This market is busier than the one at home. Animals and people converge, push against each other. The men on horseback dismount. Awa is given back; her wrists are bound again. “Move,” someone says, prodding us into groups. “They’re watching us,” I whisper. People pass by, but their heads turn and stare at us as they do. Children point and laugh. Neene frowns, confused. “Just stay close,” she says. The rope still binds us. Some of the men move. I watch them walk away and wonder where they go. Dried blood spatters stain the back of one man’s robes. I wonder whose blood and swallow back fear. A man steps in front of Takko, presses a gourd to her mouth. She is not ready; water spills onto her chin and she starts coughing, moving her head back. Then he’s in front of me. He smells of dust and cattle. The gourd presses against my mouth. He pours too fast, but the water feels cold against my cracked lips. I try to gulp it down, but end up coughing, sputtering some out as Takko did. Neene drinks but turns her face aside, refusing more before she chokes. Awa. Awa lifts her hands in the rope, trying to hold the gourd. The man pulls it back angrily and then tries again, pressing it against her mouth. Awa swallows and then, when she can’t, her cheeks grow tight and I know: she’s holding it, sealing her lips so she can’t lose what she has. New men, some in headdresses, and some in wrappers and garments like ours, cluster in small groups. One tilts his head, squinting, as he looks at us all. When he nods at Binta, one of the robed men pulls her forward, removes the rope from around her wrist and walks her toward the small group. A man walks around her; he speaks and she holds her hands out, turns them over. Neene makes a small sound; her fingers squeeze around my palm. I look up in time to see her shaking her head violently and murmuring, “No, no, no.” Her eyes flit from the man looking at Binta’s hands to the crowded market around us. A foot slides forward against the ground; the rope tugs. “Allah,” she whispers. But when the villager shrugs and nods, Neene changes. She grips our hands tighter, pulls us closer to her; her nostrils flare. Fear buds deep in my belly, but I don’t know why. “Don’t look up, don’t look up,” she says in the do as I say now voice she uses when Awa doesn’t want to do chores. Awa and I bend our heads. My shoulders curl and I shuffle my feet back a step, trying to hide behind her. The earth is darker where I stand than at home. Still yellow, but cold, not the warm shade of gold Samba and I buried. Hints of a reddish color blend. I don’t lift my head but when someone cries out, I raise only my eyes. Someone else is led forward away from the stone wall where we stand. My eyes drop again because Neene said don’t look up . I haven’t done anything right. I didn’t run. I didn’t look for Samba. And when boots appear in front of us, I look up. Neene talks over the man, shaking her head, lifting mine and Awa’s arms. Suddenly, the tall man, the one with the gun around his chest, grips her upper arm and hauls her forward. Neene looks at me. Her eyes are wider than they’ve ever been and she wails, her face long and desperate. “ Your sister,” she says in a voice I’ve never heard from her. “ Your sister, Aïssata.” “Yes, Neene.” I nod, promising her, but I don’t know what I’m promising. She is pulled in front of us, where Binta was taken. The man’s skin is brown, but lighter than ours. I don’t understand his words, and neither does Neene, because she doesn’t move. He reaches out, pulls her arm out to the side. Within moments, he nods. Something deep inside of me cracks when Awa screams and tries to run toward Neene. The rope won’t let her. Neene calls our names, over and over and over, as they bind her wrists again and lead her away from us. I can still hear her screaming even when she’s swallowed by the crowd. My mind blanks. Your sister, Aïssata! I nod to myself, moving closer to Awa. She is shouting, “Where is she? Where is she, Aïssata?” Tears spill from over my nose and into my mouth. The men look over at us and fear explodes. Don’t look up, don’t look up. “Shh shh,” I whisper frantically. “Look down, look down, Awa, please.” And something hot and awful blooms inside me. A knowing. Panic swells until I feel like I’m going to explode like the gunshots did in the village. I drop my head as low as I can and lift the rope. When I feel the pendant hanging from my neck, I curl my fingers around its edges and yank, fast and hard, until the cord snaps. Beads fall. Awa’s fingers close around it before I tell her to take it. Boots. Awa doesn’t scream when he pulls her. But I do. My whole body starts shaking and I rush forward, as far as the rope will let me and, when it pulls me back, I go to my knees. Fire. My whole body feels like someone took a torch to it. I can’t see for the tears. They make me angry because I need to see where she goes. I need to see who takes her, but I don’t see. All I see is Awa. Her hair isn’t in cornrows anymore. Fuzzy curls spring by her ears; her nightshift is covered in dust, dirt and more. I stare at her, screaming her name until my throat hurts. I shift and something hard rolls against my knee. One of the blue beads. Dirtied by earth, I pick it up, frozen, unable to look away. Don’t look up, don’t look up. The bead changes colors depending on where I look: some spots are smeared with tan streaks of dirt; others are almost clear. I use my thumb to roll it against my first finger. “Stand up and walk.” Where is she? Heat swells in my body again; my hands curl. They look at hands. Quick, while I walk, I cover my mouth, parting my lips and slipping the blue bead between them. It clicks against my teeth as I bury it beneath my tongue. The man standing in front of me is tall. His skin is dark, like mine, but with hints of olive. He stares at me and I cannot read his eyes: they are dark but they don’t have my starburst lines. I can’t see light in them. He does not move or speak. But he watches me like no one has ever done. He cocks his head to the side, walks around me. He steps close. He smells different. Tobacco and river. He holds his palm out, turns it over, nods at me. I do what the others have done: hold my arms out, straight in front of me, turn my palms over. He steps even closer, bares his teeth at me, pointing to his own mouth. I smile, wondering what he thinks about the gap between my teeth. When two of his fingers reach out, I jerk back, but he captures my chin and turns my head to the left. Neene gripped my chin. “Run!” I can’t. When he turns my head to the other side, looking at every inch of my face, something I’ve never felt rushes over me. It’s cold and the shaking grows worse. I press my tongue down against the bead. The man moves his head close, staring at my eyes. I stop breathing. He lowers his gaze slowly, dragging it over my neck and shoulders until my teeth rattle. That’s when I see it. Just beyond him, the white tent. It flutters into a gazelle running fast, its white neck stretched long. Its coat is the same tawny color of the golden dirt at home; its white belly soft as a cloud. Two long, ribbed horns stand proudly between its ears. And he runs. My chest opens; the bubbles pop one by one until air fills my lungs. I can feel the wind against my skin, blowing through my uncombed, unbraided hair. He leaps over a large puddle. While he’s suspended in mid-air, long, thin legs reaching for the safe side, it’s like he flies. The birds don’t sing. The frogs don’t splash into the current. Everything holds its breath. When his front legs strike the earth, it shakes. Then his back legs touch down. And then he’s off again, running, running, running and nobody knows where he’s going. Around him, there is only sand and patches of earth overturned. The sound of laughter confuses me. I try to stay with the gazelle, but my vision clears just as my arms drop to my sides. My arms drop to my sides . The muscles hurt to move. Carefully, I roll my shoulder and lift my arm. It really is free of the rope. Somehow, I’m sitting beneath shade, watching the man with the good teeth and clean hands talk to someone else, point to me. The tents are farther away now. I watch the crowds from a hill and scan the faces for Awa. caption: “Scars of Victory: A Memoir” by Julie Wainwright CW : abuse, rape Everyone has a story to tell, and I suppose many of them are pretty much the same. We deal with good and bad, with pain and pleasure, with the good and the not-so-good. Such is life. It’s not easy and not for the faint of heart. It’s about forging on, surviving, and then some. What I mean is that there is more to life than survival. Animals can survive, but humans can thrive and excel beyond trauma. Yes, I’ve had a tough life, marked by physical and emotional violence, yet also by incredible resilience. God instructs the heart through pain and contradictions. I am one of the fortunate ones, having made it through with maturity, confidence, and a passion for life. Help was there when I needed it. Help was there when I asked for it. A good friend once told me that a healthy person will ask for help. I agree. And I am proud to stand among the healthy ones. I had a lot of childhood trauma, but somehow found the inner strength to endure. I live in a small town in Georgia, where everyone knows everyone else and either knows, suspects, or gossips about their neighbors’ dark family secrets. I have far too many hearts to protect to focus on my own. For my story, I changed names, places, and occupations. Those do not matter. What matters are the emotions that consumed me, nearly destroyed me, and eventually led to my salvation. My dad owned his own business, a small farm supply store. To support our family of six, he worked late into the evenings and was not home very much. When he was not home, horrible things happened. I guess bad things happen like that when there is no family authority, and children are vulnerable to violent predators and sadistic tormentors. Many people choose to numb their pain with drugs and alcohol or through addictive behaviors like sex, eating, shopping, or having numerous relationships. I didn’t do that, but I found ways to numb myself. In my most private self, I shut down when I’m hurt or overwhelmed. I’ve always done this since I was a young child. I’ve always been independent and strong. I had to be. I started working at 15 and bought my first car, a 1984 Mustang GT, at 16. I left home at 17. That was the easy part. It felt so good to be independent and rely only on myself. I always had the confidence to pursue my goals and develop what I truly believe is my most incredible gift—the gift of connecting with people, listening and understanding, and expressing empathy. I am a Registered Nurse. At work, Nurse Julie is very assertive and outspoken. It doesn’t matter whether the situation involves staff or a patient. I’m assertive if need be. I can stand in front of a crowd and teach a class with confidence. Empathy and compassion led me to nursing school. I wanted to help others and be there for them, perhaps because of the love that I lacked in my childhood. Peace and love are all I want. I was taught that I was responsible for creating a beautiful life, and I let go of all drama many, many years ago. I spent years quietly stepping away from spaces and relationships that drained my energy, attending support and grief counseling groups, and reading self-help books. All of this helped transform me into a strong, independent, and exciting human being who is grounded, connected, and loved. I love life. I love people. I love myself. My twin sister, Christina, was also a Registered Nurse and was loved by many. She and my dad were both diagnosed with terminal cancers. My twin and I were inseparable, and I threw myself into caring for her and Dad. They both ended up in the same hospice facility, just months apart. I was with them both when they took their last breath. I was alone with Dad when he passed away in my arms. To the end, I was definitely a daddy’s girl, looking at the world through his kind eyes. Christina fought for ten years against an aggressive cancer called Synovial Cell Carcinoma and underwent a left above-the-knee amputation, almost to the hip. She endured several brain tumors, four craniotomies, and endless years of chemotherapy and radiation. I thought I was prepared when she had to leave us, but I wasn’t. When she passed away, it felt like half my soul was sucked out of me. I grieved heavily for years. I lost my best friend. My mother was an out-of-control alcoholic who mentally and physically traumatized me. She was cold and emotionally distant. Our home didn’t feel safe. I learned to make myself as small and quiet as possible, so I wouldn’t trigger her or bring even more chaos into the home. She did everything she could to destroy my self-esteem and self-image. Her failure to protect me forced me to endure in a house of horror. She beat me daily with a belt. She told me daily that she wished I had never been born. Dad told me that Mom was very jealous of my twin and me since we were born, and being the daddy’s girl of the home, I was her target. She looked at me through hateful eyes. At 12 years old, my brother raped me three separate times. My Mom stood and watched the third time, doing nothing. I threatened to tell Dad, and she said she would kill me. I believed her because of the physical abuse she inflicted on me over the years. At 12, I weighed only 56 pounds, and I was emotionally destroyed. It wasn’t until Christina and I were 25 that I told her what had happened, and she said it happened to her as well. My brother is now 57, with end-stage cirrhosis. I don’t talk to him. I never told my dad what my brother did to me, and neither did Christina, for fear of what he would do. My dad was in the Army. There were guns in the home, and he would have killed my brother. My Dad has been gone for ten years, and I promised him I would take care of my mother. Since Dad’s passing, she had five major surgeries and, at 84, is frail and temperamental. I had several opportunities to place her in a rehabilitation facility, but after each surgery, I broke my promise to Dad and brought her home from the hospital. Even though she was verbally abusive, I gave her care from a clinical perspective, which protected our boundaries. I separated my role as her child from my duties as her caregiver. I treated her as my patient, rather than as my mother, and provided medical support without being overwhelmed by personal grief. But today, as I write these words, I’m alive and in love with myself and the world. It sounds strange, but to reach where I am now, I had to crawl over shards of glass, bleeding from pain and degradation, to make it to the other side. I was taught that I was no more than an animal, a feral one in a world without love. I’m older, wiser, and stronger now, but only after enduring a childhood hell in which I was brainwashed into believing I was a mistake. I wanted to tell my story in a plain, honest voice and trust the truth to be enough. I suppose my story has come full circle: although I was not loved or protected, I was able to provide love and protection in the end. I did not run away from my pain. I embraced it as I created a world of love and safety and a life filled with contemplation and creativity. I love my life, the good and the not-so-good. Life is not perfect, but our attitude can help us navigate the harsh storms. People need people. I have family, friends, and a special friend who believes in me and has changed my life for the better. What is different about me now? My perspective, for one, has changed. I am aware of my past and my present. Both are real, and each carries its own distinctive dollop of pain and misery. Life is like that. Everyone gets burned, and we all feel the pain. I can’t change the past. I didn’t make it happen, and I didn’t want it to happen. But I made it through, and I am safe now. I’m a mature middle-aged woman, and my mother cannot hurt me. I want to share my message. You can make it, too. That’s the message that I want to share. Nothing more. Nothing less. If it’s not the truth, I do not speak it, and the truth will set you free. caption: Understanding Trauma: Insights from “The Body Keeps the Score” Bessel van der Kolk’s groundbreaking book, The Body Keeps the Score: Brain, Mind, and Body in the Healing of Trauma , has become a cornerstone in the understanding of trauma and its profound impact on human beings. This book bridges the gap between science, personal experience, and therapeutic practice, shedding light on how trauma reshapes the body and the mind. It empowers us with a transformative understanding of trauma. Reading this book changed my life and gave me hope that pharmaceutical companies haven’t completely taken over the field of psychology and that there are other ways to heal that have been studied decades ago. Understanding Trauma Van der Kolk begins by defining trauma as not just the events that happened but the lasting effects these events have on the mind and body. Trauma stems from deeply distressing or disturbing experiences that overwhelm an individual’s capacity to cope. He explains that trauma is more than a memory—it’s an ongoing physical and emotional reaction. Survivors of trauma often relive their experiences in vivid ways, sometimes decades after the event. How Trauma Affects the Brain One of the key revelations in The Body Keeps the Score is how trauma alters the brain’s functioning. Van der Kolk discusses three main areas of the brain affected by trauma: The Reptilian Brain (brainstem) is responsible for survival instincts. It becomes overactive in trauma survivors, leading to heightened states of fight, flight, or freeze. The Limbic System : This emotional center of the brain, including the amygdala, becomes hyperactive, causing heightened emotional reactions and difficulty regulating feelings. The Prefrontal Cortex : Often referred to as the “rational brain,” this area shuts down under trauma, impairing the ability to think logically and self-regulate. Van der Kolk illustrates how trauma keeps the brain stuck in a state of alarm, which explains the overwhelming emotions, flashbacks, and triggers experienced by survivors. The Body Remembers One of the book’s central ideas is that trauma is stored in the body. Van der Kolk emphasizes that physical sensations, muscle tension, and autonomic nervous system responses often carry the imprint of traumatic experiences. Survivors might not consciously recall their trauma, but their bodies frequently relive it through chronic pain, digestive issues, autoimmune disorders, or other physical symptoms. For example, someone who has experienced assault might flinch at physical touch, or a survivor of war might feel a constant state of hypervigilance. These bodily reactions are ways the body remembers and protects itself from perceived threats. The Role of Dissociation Van der Kolk highlights dissociation as a common coping mechanism for trauma survivors. Dissociation occurs when individuals detach from their physical and emotional experiences to survive overwhelming situations. While helpful now, it often leads to long-term disconnection from one’s body and emotions. Many trauma survivors report feelings of numbness, a sense of unreality, or even memory loss surrounding the traumatic event. This disconnection can make recovery challenging, as it impedes the integration of traumatic memories. Healing Trauma: The Mind-Body Connection Van der Kolk’s book is not just about understanding trauma but also about healing it. He advocates for a holistic approach that addresses both the mind and body. Traditional talk therapy, while valuable, is often insufficient for deeply entrenched trauma. Instead, he suggests incorporating body-focused and experiential therapies. Key modalities discussed include: Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing (EMDR): EMDR uses guided eye movements to help individuals process and integrate traumatic memories. Yoga and Body Awareness: Trauma disrupts the connection between the mind and body. Yoga helps survivors regain control over their bodies and fosters a sense of safety. Neurofeedback: By training the brain to regulate itself, neurofeedback can help reduce symptoms of trauma, such as anxiety and hypervigilance. Theater and Expressive Arts: Creative outlets like acting allow survivors to express and process emotions in a safe environment. Mindfulness and Meditation: These practices promote present-moment awareness, helping survivors reduce stress and reconnect with their bodies. The Importance of Relationships in Healing Van der Kolk emphasizes the pivotal role of safe and supportive relationships in trauma recovery. Trauma often stems from interpersonal violations, and healing requires restoring trust and connection. He discusses the importance of empathetic and validating environments, whether through therapists, friends, family, or support groups. This underscores the importance of your support in the recovery process. Trauma in Society The book also explores the broader implications of trauma, particularly its prevalence in marginalized communities and its impact on societal systems such as healthcare, education, and criminal justice. Van der Kolk argues that understanding trauma is essential for creating compassionate systems that support healing rather than perpetuating harm. The Body Keeps the Score is more than a book—it’s a call to action. Van der Kolk’s work underscores the importance of recognizing trauma in individual lives and society. By acknowledging the profound ways trauma affects the body and brain, we open the door to innovative and compassionate approaches to healing. Whether you’re a trauma survivor, a caregiver, or a mental health professional, Van der Kolk’s insights provide a roadmap for understanding and addressing the long-lasting effects of trauma. The message is clear: healing is not just a possibility; it’s a reality, and it begins with honoring the connection between the body, mind, and soul. This instills a sense of hope and optimism in the journey of recovery. The Brain’s Role: Trauma rewires the brain, keeping survivors in a state of hyperarousal and emotional reactivity. Healing Requires Integration: Recovery involves reconnecting the mind and body and integrating traumatic memories in a way that no longer dominates a survivor’s life. Holistic Approaches Are Essential: Combining traditional psychotherapy with body-focused modalities offers the most effective path to healing. caption: Passing on this info from my therapist that I have found helpful to know. When you're having a panic attack you don't 'need to breathe'. You specifically need to breathe out. You are feeling pain because you have been breathing too shallowly and have built up too much carbon dioxide. You need to get rid of that. So you need to breathe out for longer than you are breathing in. Breathe out as long as you can, and then let your body be in charge of breathing in. Your body can, and will, do that bit for you. Repeat that as long as you feel you need. Then once you're calmer and aren't feeling the pain you can do the second thing they taught me. Imagine the air lazily entering your body and moving down to curl around in your stomach like a kitten, and then stretching up to move up and out again. This image can help to breathe deeply and slowly again. You can find a different image if another is more useful to you. Repeat as long as you like. # PanicAttack

caption: A Panic Attack May Not Be What You Think I’m going to explain to you what a panic attack is. It does not just mean experiencing a great fear or being terrified irrespective of circumstances. I’ve experienced two bouts of panic attacks in my life. I had to take Xanax to counter the attacks until time worked its magic, and the attacks ceased. A panic attack is not a feeling of panic in the face of a real danger . If you feel something is threatening is happening, and you feel panic, this is a normal response to the threat . If you can remove the threat, and your panic subsides, this is also the sign that what you are experiencing is not a panic attack. “I was watching this thing on TV and I felt I was having a panic attack. Then I turned the TV off, and I was okay.” What you were experiencing wasn’t a panic attack, it was a normal reaction to something your brain found threatening, out there, in the world. See, a panic attack is an irrational sense of fear, when there is nothing out there that can ostensibly harm you. There is nothing that you can remove from your environment to make the panic go away. A panic attack is your body thinking that there’s a threat, when there is no threat. No amount of reassurance will make the panic attack go away, because it is irrational. Your Autistic Life is supported by readers like you. Use one of the links below to support my writing! Thank you. Join Us Bonfire Merch A panic attack is very different from the first scenario I gave you above, because there is nothing short of taking medicines that will make it go away. Breathing exercises and moderate it, but they won’t eliminate it. How do I know? Again, I’ve had two bouts of panic attacks. I could look around me, and see there was nothing threatening in my environment, but my sense of panic did not go away. I could reason that there was no threat, but this rationality found no purchase in the irrationality of the panic attack. “But I was able to make my panic go away with…” If it was anything short of taking an anxiolytic, what you experienced was plain old panic , and not a panic attack . Using the incorrect language, and insisting that your plain old panic is a panic attack, is harmful in much the same that insisting that someone who experiences a bout of anxiety on a date is suffering from social anxiety, or that someone who is sad at the death of a pet is experiencing depression. People normally rebound from their anxiety or their sadness. One sure sign that what you are dealing with is not social anxiety or depression is that you can easily fix the problem. People with social anxiety, for instance, will ruminate before and after the event. People experiencing depression won’t be pulled out of depression by a joke. It is harmful in the same way that saying “we’re all a little autistic” is harmful. It is a way to minimize a real problem, a problem that cannot be merely fixed by reorganizing your world. anxiety AutisticWriters danger irrational minimization panic PanicAttack YourAutisticLife

caption: Is there really a bright side? “Always Look on the Bright Side of Life”, was coined in 1979 by Eric Idle, for the ending of the Monty Python film; Life of Brian. Sang by another man facing crucifixion in attempt to cheer up the main character, Brian, the song features lyrics that have a surprisingly deep message. In a full-circle way, the song repeats the same themes; the unfortunate parts of life, picking yourself up, and focusing on the good. Which, for a comedic and incredibly satirical film, is something we should all deeply consider. But what if there actually isn’t a bright side? Personally, I struggle a lot to remain optimistic. So much so, that 2 months ago, I got a tattoo with the phrase ‘Amor Fati’, meaning ‘Love Fate’ in Latin. But the fact I felt the need to get the tattoo alone goes to show how sometimes we do need reminders that things will work out. It’s easy to say as a pessimist, but it’s incredibly difficult to remain optimistic all the time. It’s human to have emotions and have bad days, but the most important skill to have is ‘to look on the bright side’. Although, on the flip side, we have to be wary of toxic positivity. Think of it this way: Yes, things probably will work out, and yes, it’s always beneficial to focus on the good, but it’s also important to take time to actually feel . Perhaps it’s naive to say, but I truly don’t believe we should always look for the good in a situation. I don’t believe in suppressing feelings, hiding from the truth, or ignoring problems. If we do that, how on earth do we expect to learn or move on from them? I think it’s a very human thing to do; seeing the good in the bad. And I applaud those who are able to do so. But what do we actually gain in doing so? That isn’t to say, however, that we should dwell in the bad things that happen to us – it just means we should allow ourselves to actually feel waht we’re feeling and heal, rather than make excuses and move on too quickly. And in another realm, this toxic thinking can lead us to not only dismiss our own feelings, but also the feelings of others. It can seem a simple remark, saying “don’t worry about that job turning you down, there’ll be another one”, but in reality, we’re just affirming that instead of moving forward, we’re actually moving past the issue. It’s more beneficial here, to ask your friend what they thought lead to that outcome, what could be done better, how has it left them feeling. Rather than dismissing the situation and encouraging them to dive head first into another (possibly negative) instance. This can be a very confusing topic, because ideally, we need to find a balance of the two. We need to find a way to allow ourselves to feel and accept outcomes, but also remain positive that things can move forward from it. We can’t dismiss, but we can’t dwell. We have to accept, and use it to push us forward. This is a very interesting topic to me, and something I personally struggle with, so look out for more posts with this theme: accepting outcomes .
